item.content:encoded:
Danish furniture brand OMHU has released a version of its Teddy sofa bed on third-party websites for a fraction of its usual price to draw attention to copy culture and to work as marketing.

Last weekend, the company released its own limited-edition "dupe" of the Teddy sofa. Intentionally misspelling the name and lowering the price, the brand said it wanted to bring awareness to what it views as the problem of dupes.

According to OMHU, the project is based on market research conducted after its original Teddy sofa went viral in 2022. The research established dupes sold online, and not other brands, as its biggest competitors.

"The OMHU Teddy is one of the most duped pieces of furniture out there, which is quite the compliment, but a tiring issue nonetheless," OMHU creative director Christine Smith told Dezeen.

"Normally you'd just report dupes or ignore them, but we spotted a creative opportunity to turn the issue on its head and build some global awareness around the real cost of buying cheap."

"We decided to make fun of the competition by beating them at their own game: misspelt name, selling on dupe retailers and all, while still proving a point that we're the OG of sofas".

The Tedy is a replica of the original Teddy sofa, a two-seater sofa upholstered in 90 per cent polyester, with a chrome-plated steel frame. The sofa is also modular and expands into a bed or large floor cushion.

The Tedy is made with the same materials and construction as the Teddy but upholstered in a bright "dupe-orange". It retails for $799.99 as opposed to the Teddy, which retails at $1,995.

OMHU said it set the cost based on the average price of dupes online, and sold 50 of the limited-edition sofas on websites such as Temu, Etsy and Dupe.com instead of its own website.

Instead of "pointing fingers", OMHU wanted to "outdupe them".

Read:

Planned London Design Festival installation "extremely close to my earlier projects" says Yuri Suzuki

The strategy is to meet audiences where they would normally shop for more affordable versions, according to the brand, though it's unclear how this might affect future business practices or pricing.

The 50 Tedys were released on 5 September and sold out within 10 minutes, according to OMHU.

The brand has spun out a whole marketing campaign on top of the release, including hiring lookalike influencers and hosting look alike competitions.

"The concept didn't stop with the sofa," said the brand.

"OMHU made dupe culture the entire marketing strategy, creating 'dupefluencers' – celebrity lookalike influencers recruited to launch their lookalike sofa."

"OMHU turned the trend into its own spin on influencer marketing."

Though the pattern of knock-offs is not new one, OMHU also pointed out a growth in dupe culture in connection to Gen Z and internet culture, noting the trend's expansion from fashion into furniture and design.

"Every iconic brand goes through this," said OMHU CEO Simon Salomonsson. "This isn't just our fight. We welcome any brand that is tired of being copied to join the conversation."

Dupes and copying are an ongoing issue in the design world. Emeco recently sued Zara Home for allegedly copying and selling a chair designed by Norman Foster and technology company Digby partnered with Heller on a tool that examined the authenticity of physical design products using NFTs in 2023.

The photography is courtesy of OMHU.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studios Populous and Moody Nolan have released designs for a professional basketball and hockey arena based on the shape of Philadelphia's iconic Spectrum arena.

The planned arena will serve as the home of NBA team the 76ers and the NHL team the Flyers, as well as a forthcoming WNBA team.

The planned venue will replace the Xfinity Mobile Arena, which was completed in 1996 in the South Philadelphia Sports Complex, where the city's NFL stadium is also located.

Populous and Moody Nolan designed a circular structure with concentric stacked rings. The rings, which will be slightly offset, will alternate between glazed facades and LED displays.

The teams said that the design was based on the Spectrum, an arena built in 1967 and designed by SOM that was demolished in 2011.

"The new arena will connect the next gathering place for Philadelphia sports and entertainment to one of the city's most storied sports sites for future generations," said a press release from the Flyers and 76ers.

"The arena's architecture draws inspiration from the shape of the Spectrum, which hosted the Flyers and the 76ers for nearly three decades, and reimagines it through a contemporary design lens," continued the statement.

"The exterior will be defined by stacked, cantilevered bands that break down the scale of a typical arena and create a bold, instantly recognizable profile as a new South Philadelphia landmark."

Read:

Populous designs Charlotte Hornets facility clad in "swarm" of panels

The plaza around the stadium will be dedicated to "active outdoor spaces" and the teams compared the entry stairs to other Philadelphia landmarks such as its art museum.

There will be restaurants on the half-acre of outdoor space, with the final form still pending fan feedback.

According to the joint statement from the 76ers' and Flyers' owners, Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment and Comcast Spectacor, respectively, the project is set to be the "largest fully privately funded project in the city's history".

Recently, Dezeen highlighted advances in sports architecture in our Future Stadium series.

Other recent NBA architecture news in the US includes a district around the upcoming Oklahoma City Thunder stadium.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a product aiming to give confidence and physical support to elderly travellers is among projects by students at the Basel Academy of Art and Design.

Also featured is a collection of garments, including hand-painted prints on silk and a portable, pocket-sized gaming device for people who seek sensory experiences.

Basel Academy of Art and Design

Institution: BaselFHNW University of Applied Sciences and Arts Northwestern Switzerland
Course: Masterstudio Design
Tutors: Nicole Schneider, Andreas Wenger, Shehrie Islamaj, Jacqueline Loekito and Daniel Harris

School statement:

"The Masterstudio Design at the Institute Contemporary Design Practices (ICDP) is composed of three studios: Masterstudio Industrial Design, Masterstudio Scenography and Masterstudio Fashion Design.

"Each studio has a disciplinary focus. In addition, the research discourse of the ICDP focuses on Digital Integration, Design Cultures and Circular Design and are reflected and communicated multidimensionally.

"The basis of our applied research and project work is the design term 'advanced design'.

"Instead of the current economic practice of maximisation, we adopt the role of the extrapreneur in teaching and design, which stands for collaboration and systemic action.

"Current issues on global crises, climate change and social inequality are discussed and further developed.

"Sustainability and ecology, inclusion and technology, interaction and materiality are the fields in which the role of design is questioned and new visions for human coexistence and economic activity are defined.

"The Masterstudio Design offers in-depth training in professional, future-oriented design practice and applied research.

"Relevant research questions are identified and defined, appropriate and complex design processes are conceived, projects are developed and implemented.

"Communication, project management, cross-disciplinary and research-oriented teamwork are components of the training."

Etwas ist geblieben – Fabers Kammer by Alexander Prekas

"Drawing on theoretical research and interviews with artists, I examine how narrative spaces create sensory experiences, shift perspectives and offer temporary detachment from digital life.

"Building on these findings, I developed etwas ist geblieben – Fabers Kammer, an immersive narrative space inspired by Fahrenheit 451.

"Through a 1:1 installation, visitors enter Faber's chamber, explore objects, sounds, and smells, and gradually reconstruct his story.

"The work addresses censorship, digital desensitisation, and the need for conscious, sensory experiences."

Student: Alexander Prekas
Course: Studio Scenography
Mentors: Andreas Wegener, Martina Ehleiter and Ruth Scheel

Triggering Ritual: Ceramic as a Multisensory Design Medium by Boyun Choi

"Ceramic defines the modern bathroom yet remains largely unnoticed.

"This research investigates why ceramic has become invisible despite its presence and explores its potential as a multisensory design medium for ritual self-care.

"Drawing on multisensory perception, embodied memory and ritual formation, the study examines ceramics' tactile, acoustic and visual qualities.

"A survey of 60 participants, alongside interviews with two specialists at Laufen, reveals a gap between ceramics' sensory potential and its current use.

"The research identifies three conditions for ceramic to trigger ritual: sensory presence, consistency and intentionality, reframing the bathroom as a space where material, body and habit converge."

Student: Boyun Choi
Course: Studio Industrial Design
Tutors: Nicole Schneider, Werner Baumhakl, Pia Scharf and Naïma Trabelsi

The Center of Her World by Bruna Ideias

"A modular furniture system for the birthing room, currently in development.

"My project challenges the delivery bed as the default centrepiece of the maternity ward, a form that signals rest and passivity regardless of position, even when builtfor multiple postures.

"Working with two midwives, I am exploring how warm tones, soft curves and natural materials could prime the body for movement and verticality, replacing scattered aids like the solitary birthing ball or stool.

"Rather than proposing one object, my goal is to offer a platform for autonomy, making the birthing person, not the bed, the centre of the room."

Student: Bruna Ideias
Course: Studio Industrial Design
Tutor: Nicole Schneider

Plant Intimacies by Elisa Bartat

"This thesis examines how natural history museums display nature and how scenographic practices can reinforce anthropocentric narratives.

"Drawing on ecological relationality and more-than-human theories, it investigates how exhibition spaces shape knowledge and frame relationships between humans and the natural world.

"The research identifies anthropocentrism as a systemic condition within museum display, situated between control and care.

"In response, Plant Intimacies proposes an open, living installation that dissolves the vitrine and brings plants and people together.

"Plants are presented not as objects, but as relational agents, offering an intimate way to experience ecological belonging through sensory encounter."

Student: Elisa Bartat
Course: Studio Scenography
Tutors: Charlotte Tamschick, Martina Ehleiter and Ruth Scheel

Valere by Elvira Grau

"This collection explores value and appreciation through fashion as a multisensory experience that fosters emotional connection and empowerment.

"Inspired by daily life, nature and life cycles, it presents fashion as an expressive language.

"The work combines sculptural silhouettes, hand-painted silk prints, and detailed craftsmanship, with a special focus on footwear design and the transformation of existing shoes.

"Traditional St Gallen embroidery connects Swiss textile heritage with contemporary design.

"Conceived from head to toe, the looks create immersive silhouettes that unite individuality, preciousness and contemporary storytelling."

Student: Elvira Grau
Course: Studio Fashion
Tutors: Priska Morger, Jörg Wiese and Ruth Scheel

Fragments of Waldenburg by Lia Schürpf

"This project was developed in collaboration with Kaserne Basel and the Masterstudio Scenography (FHNW).

"For the site-specific parcours Waldenburg (12-14 June 2026), I created four participatory scenographic installations.

"They invite residents and visitors to actively shape the experience before, during, and after the parcours.

"Drawing on Waldenburg's existing visual landscape, the works transform familiar elements and reveal them in new contexts, encouraging audiences to experience the place from a fresh perspective."

Student: Lia Schürpf
Course: Studio Scenography
Tutors: Andreas Wenger and Martina Ehleiter

MDK by Miranda Kistler

"With a mixed cultural background and a background in photography and art, I wondered what we hold on to deeply when in constant flux?

"Every object is a vessel for a memory we fear losing. Yet, constant shift transforms us into curators of our lives.

"We learn the profound act of intentional loss, leaving valuable fragments in specific places as anchors, as reminders of where we root our sense of home and a promise that we will eventually return.

"My design practice is born from this fluid existence. Designing with intention and functionality, creating work that is not only rooted in change but explicitly meant to be changed.

"In the beauty of transformation is where memory truly lives.

"By weaving interconnections and braiding disparate stories together into garments, design becomes a way of operating, an interlaced, intertwined web that helps us exist within a complicated world."

Student: Miranda Kistler
Course: Studio Fashion
Tutor: Jacqueline Loekito

All These Open Windows But No Fresh Air by Nada Elghareb

"The project presents a portable, pocket-sized sensory hunting game. The game aims to ground the player in the physical world through tactile tasks.

"It functions either as a standalone screen-free companion or as a magnetic attachment for your smartphone."

Student: Nada Elghareb
Course: Studio Industrial Design

Noerah by Noerah

"The NOERAH FW26 debut collection plays with the idea of 'accessorise until you're dressed' as both method and attitude.

"It is an exploration of accessories not as additions, but as the starting point from which garments emerge.

"NOERAH's world revolves around wearable objects, attachments and bodily extensions that activate and involve the body.

"Influenced by electronic music, club culture, post-human feminism and avatar-based styling games, the collection proposes a universe of wearable fantasies, shifting identities, synthetic glamour and collective imagination."

Student: Noerah
Course: Studio Fashion
Tutors: Jacqueline Loekito, Prof. Priska Morger and Ruth Scheel

MOOVE – A new perspective on mobility for older adults by Lorenzo Rimini

"Aging is often treated as a problem to solve rather than a natural phase of life. Yet society remains largely designed around young, able-bodied users, creating dependency and reduced confidence among older adults.

"MOOVE responds to this gap by introducing an 'aging travel companion' for active travellers aged 75 plus. Positioned between luggage and a walker, it combines walking support, a perching seat and contemporary aesthetics.

"Each function supports a sense of autonomy: stability enables confidence, seating provides reliability and personalisation preserves dignity. Rather than assisting users as patients, MOOVE empowers them to travel independently, confidently and with style."

Student: Lorenzo Rimini
Course: Studio Industrial Design

item.content:encoded:
A sweeping white roof informed by the pages of a book crowns Chang'an Academy Xi'an Public Library, a cultural centre in Shanxi Province.

Overlooking the Ba River and Olympic Sports Centre in Xi'an's Chanba Ecological Area, the 70,000-square-metre complex contains spaces for reading, exhibitions and education.

It was designed by Chinese studios Hong Designworks and China Northwest Architectural Design and Research Institute.

The design team looked to balance the project's role as a large-scale public landmark with spaces that would feel welcoming and accessible to visitors, describing their approach as a process of "de-memorialisation."

"Our inspiration came from observing a shift in how public cultural architecture is being discussed today," Hong Designworks co-founder Ming Dang told Dezeen.

"The focus is no longer solely on formal expression, but increasingly on how spaces invite everyday use."

"The vitality of cultural architecture, we believe, lies not in scale alone, but in its capacity to sustain genuine, everyday connections between people and the city," Dang continued.

In order to help break down the scale of the building, it is divided into three sections by a central plaza and a long, narrow cut made through its centre, drawing both visitors and daylight into a large atrium.

According to Hong Designworks, this atrium was designed to encourage a wide range of activities, from quieter working areas and reading nooks to amphitheatre-style spaces for larger gatherings.

These are organised across a variety of levels and connected by curved staircases and walkways.

Read:

Sinuous form of Shenzhen Natural History Museum emulates "a piece of landscape"

"In many large-scale public buildings, atria are often conceived as monumental voids – spaces intended primarily for circulation rather than lingering," said Dang.

"The project breaks away from this 'large but empty' spatial logic, transforming the atrium into an engaging environment that encourages gathering, pause, and interaction."

Enhancing the feeling of openness in these spaces is the library's sweeping roof, which is lower at the building's centre and rises upwards in its corners above full-height glazed walls.

As well as evoking the pages of an open book, this form was chosen as a nod to the upturned eaves found in traditional Chinese architecture.

Wood-grain metal panels were used throughout the interiors to satisfy fire requirements while maintaining a feeling of warmth, alongside stone floors and ceilings clad in white triangular panels.

Other libraries in China recently featured in Dezeen include the Beijing City Library by Snøhetta, which features a roof designed to emulate the feeling of "sitting under a tree", and a library designed to resemble a shell made from bricks.

The photography is courtesy of Studio Ten.

item.content:encoded:
Paint brand Dulux has announced Soulful Sage – "a versatile green that provides a flexible foundation for schemes" – as its colour of the year for 2027.

Dulux selected the soft grey-green as its annual colour of the year as it is a calm shade that has clear connections to nature.

"Taking us straight back to nature, it's a calm, uplifting shade – just what's needed today," the brand said.

The selection is the result of research carried out throughout the year by the paint brand's parent company AkzoNobel. According to the brand, sage is a soothing and versatile colour, chosen as a response to the current feelings of global uncertainty.

"To deliver projects that add lasting value, architects, specifiers and designers must consider how colour can support the intended purpose of a space, its functionality and the experience of the people using it," said Dulux.

"AkzoNobel's annual ColourFutures research helps to inform this by translating emerging social and design trends into a practical colour direction that professionals can interpret and adapt for real projects."

Read:

Rhythm of Blues named Dulux Colour of the Year 2026

"For 2027, the research identified a move towards lighter, more considered environments that respond to the information overload and wider global uncertainty that people are experiencing," the brand continued.

"These insights shaped Soulful Sage, a versatile green that provides a flexible foundation for schemes requiring different levels of warmth, neutrality or visual energy, depending on the brief."

Last year Dulux selected a trio of blue colours named Rhythm of Blues, as its Colour of the Year.

Rival colour arbiter Pantone, meanwhile, picked an understated, greyish white hue called Cloud Dancer.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: HIMACS has added five colourways to its terrazzo-inspired collection, which have received a prestigious Red Dot Design Award 2026 in the product category.

The HIMACS Terrazzo collection reimagines a timeless material technique through rich textures, a carefully balanced colour palette and distinctive, mineral-inspired patterns.

The five additional HIMACS Terrazzo colours include Terrazzo Ulivo, Terrazzo Nuvola, Terrazzo Sorrento, Terrazzo Marsala and Terrazzo Selva.

The latest colours have been recognised with the award, which celebrates the contemporary reinterpretation of traditional aesthetics, combining expressive design with responsible material innovation.

The hues incorporate SCS-certified pre-consumer recycled content, demonstrating how the demands of modern design can successfully coexist with enhanced sustainability in a high-performance solid surface.

The result is a versatile surface solution suited to hospitality, retail, workplace and residential environments. It also boasts the same aesthetics, durability and ease-of-maintenance that terrazzo is famous for.

"The integration of production offcuts, recovered and reintroduced into new formulations during the fabrication process, supports a more circular approach to manufacturing," said Martin Saxby, director of HIMACS UK.

"Among the awarded colours, Terrazzo Selva stands out with 25 per cent recycled content, one of the highest levels currently available within our extensive portfolio," Saxby added.

"Safety is a further consideration when specifying materials, and HIMACS is entirely free of silica, nanoparticles, formaldehyde and VOCs," he continued.

item.content:encoded:
Polish-American architect Daniel Libeskind has been named architecture laureate for this year's Praemium Imperiale awards by the Japan Art Association.

Libeskind, who leads the New York-based Studio Libeskind and is one of the judges for this year's Dezeen Awards, was selected for the award for his work creating "emotionally resonant, innovative, and sustainable" architecture.

"Daniel Libeskind is an internationally renowned architect and urban designer, celebrated for his ability to evoke cultural memory through emotionally resonant and original architecture," the Japan Art Association said.

"Guided by a deep passion for music, philosophy, and literature, Libeskind creates architecture that is emotionally resonant, innovative, and sustainable."

Born in Łódź, Poland, in 1946, Libeskind is known for his deconstructionist style, which favours sharp angles and geometric structures.

Notable projects by the architect include the Jewish Museum Berlin in 2001 and Bundeswehr Museum of Military History in 2011.

More recently, the studio completed the Maggie's Centre at the Royal Free in London and the Atrium at Sumner in Brooklyn, New York.

Alongside his built works, the awarding body also praised Libeskind's wider contributions to architectural education and his influence on shaping cultural spaces.

"Libeskind is also a prominent voice in the field, frequently speaking at universities and professional conferences on the art and impact of architecture," the Japan Art Association said.

"His work and ideas have been featured in numerous exhibitions and publications, shaping contemporary architectural discourse and influencing the evolution of cities and cultural spaces."

Libeskind will receive an honorarium of 15 million yen (£70,000) as the winner of the architecture award, which is given out annually by the Japan Art Association under the patronage of Prince Hitachi, younger brother to the emperor emeritus of Japan.

Read:

Kengo Kuma awarded Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award by CDA

The Praemium Imperiale is an annual global arts prize that celebrates creatives in the fields of architecture, painting, sculpture, music, theatre and film.

Named alongside Libeskind as this year's winners are actor Cate Blanchett for theatre and film and artists Herbert Blomstedt for music, Andy Goldsworthy for sculpture and Jenny Holzer for painting. All were praised for their creative impact on society.

"This year's laureates share an immense passion for their respective craft as well as the land and people that inspire their art," Praemium Imperiale's International Advisor in the UK Lord Patten of Barnes said.

"Together their body of work celebrates the beauty and transformative power of art for the individual and the society."

Alongside the Praemium Imperiale Awards, the Japan Art Association selected children's art network La Source Garouste for the 2026 Grant for Young Artists.

Previous winners of the award's architecture category include Eduardo Souto de Moura, Shigeru Ban and Diébédo Francis Kéré.

The photography is by Roland Horn, courtesy of the Japan Art Association, unless otherwise stated.

item.content:encoded:
Students at Finland's Aalto University have collaborated with Dutch pram brand Bugaboo to create a pushchair using bio-based and biodegradable materials.

Amsterdam brand Bugaboo originally approached Aalto University during last year's Dutch Design Week, where the school presented an exhibition of experimental biomaterials.

To translate some of this biomaterial innovation into a functioning product, students from the Espoo institution's multidisciplinary chemarts course joined forces with the design team at Bugaboo.

The result is a version of the brand's stroller that's decked out in biodegradable materials but retains Bugaboo's classic black metal frame, including the wheels and seat belts.

"Sometimes, it's the unexpected or seemingly crazy ideas that open up new possibilities and start important conversations," Aalto University design lecturer Anna-Marie van der Lei told Dezeen.

"We need to imagine and experiment with what our future material world could look like, whether that means creating canopies from peels or foams from egg cartons."

Chemical engineering student Nikolai Kurochkin developed a composite material of sawdust and methyl cellulose that forms a sandy-hued back panel for the pushchair. Methyl cellulose is a compound derived from plant cellulose that can be used as a thickener and emulsifier.

The brown-coloured, plant-based leather seat cover was created by Alois Auer and Renata Khayrutdinova, who coated the material in tar to make it as water-repellent as possible.

"The students developed the tar coating that gives the seat a pleasant scent as well as durability," explained bio products lecturer Tiina Nypelö.

"With fully biodegradable materials, achieving water resistance is challenging," added van der Lei, who conceded that a fully waterproof biomaterial pram is still a work in progress.

The seat cover was inlaid with a mixture of materials to provide cushioning. Starch-based foam by Nooa Laisalmi was combined with recycled fibre-foam stuffing created by Elisabeth Baidoo from egg cartons that would have otherwise been thrown away.

Read:

Finnish company launches "world's most carbon-storing building material"

For the pram's woven canopy, Serranur Zileli developed a light brown material made from waste orange peel, which emits a subtle citrusy smell.

Julia Särkkä designed a delicate, biolace blanket in the same colour using hemp and lignin – one of the key polymers that give strength and durability to plant cell walls.

The pushchair's product labels are also cellulose-based, developed by Alessandra Fini, Bianca-Elena Galan and Cathrin Simbikangwa.

The pram was developed in Aalto University's Chemarts laboratory, with each student using specific processes and equipment depending on the biomaterial they were conceiving.

While the pushchair is currently only a concept model, the lecturers said that working with Bugaboo offered students the chance to work in a real-world context.

"Students had opportunities to meet with Bugaboo's design lead and engineer and discuss their experiments," said Van der Lei.

"Bugaboo gave us a lot of freedom, and the final stroller was developed by students who chose to continue working on the project themselves."

Known for championing biomaterials, researchers at Aalto University recently salvaged 300-year-old wood from the wreckage of a cargo ship in Oulu, which was transformed into yarn and knitted into a zero-waste dress.

A slew of other projects exploring the potential of cellulose have been showcased at the institution in previous years.

The photography is by Esa Kapila, courtesy of Aalto University.

Chairs made of wood lacquer and a lighting installation informed by paper-twining were among the highlights of the In Situ exhibition during Design Miami Seoul.

Taking place from 31 August to 6 September, this year's Design Miami Seoul was held at Design Lab within the Zaha Hadid-designed Dongdaemun Design Plaza.

Its In Situ exhibition spotlighted Korean design from both emerging and established studios, spanning lighting, furniture, ceramics, and sculptural design.

Here Dezeen selects seven of the most interesting designs from In Situ:

Biiit collection by Mano Design Studio

This brass structure was designed to be a contemporary reinterpretation of traditional Korean candlesticks, with paper made from raw mulberry bark  stitched around the frame.

Seoul-based Mano Design Studio was founded by Bo Ah Kim in 2016, who works at the intersection of traditional Korean craft and contemporary design.

"The Biiit collection seeks to dissolve the hierarchy between maker and material in an era of uniform mass replication," said Kim.

"Through a relational resonance built on mutual engagement, it aims to restore design's inherent, tactile 'thingness'."

Narrative series, by Byungsub Kim

Seoul-based furniture designer Byungsub Kim designed a chair, shelving unit and bench for his Narrative series collection.

Kim combined stainless steel with Korean mother of pearl lacquerware – a traditional craft in which wood is lacquered and inlaid with mother of pearl – for the pieces.

"The Narrative series illuminates the tension that exists among the passage of time harboured within materials, the remnants of discarded functions, and their newly bestowed roles," said Kim.

After Inage series and White Nostalgia series, by Hyunhee Kim

Artist Hyunhee Kim developed a series of furniture informed by traditional Korean furniture and gyubang culture – the material and domestic culture associated with women's quarters in the traditional Korean home.

For the pieces, she deconstructed classical furniture forms and combined contemporary sculptural language with modern materials such as acrylic and aluminium, creating a dialogue between past and present.

Nodus, by Il Hoon Roh

Nodus is a lighting installation by Seoul-based architect Il Hoon Roh, which was informed by Korean's traditional paper-twining technique that first appeared in the 12th century.

Contemporary materials such as carbon fibre was combined with the heritage craft. Individual strands were twisted into knots which then accumulated to form a surface.

The work was created through the repetitive act of knotting, in reference to the name of the piece Nodus, which means knot in Latin.

"The series represent both an artistic investigation into the evolving relationship between these disciplines and a compelling synthesis of traditional craftsmanship and cutting-edge contemporary materials," said Roh.

Guseul by WKND Lab

Design studio WKND Lab's Guseul (sphere in Korean) is a lighting installation that featured a series of balls crafted by various traditional Korean techniques.

The black balls were made using Ottchil and mother of pearl, traditional wood lacquer inlaid with mother of pearl, while the red Chil-bo balls used a glass enamel technique and were made in collaboration with artisan Jeongkeun Park.

Founded by Eunji Jun and Halin Lee, WKND Lab aims to preserve traditional values by integrating them into contemporary work.

"Guseul embodies the journey from a single dot to a profound line, symbolising the connection of diverse elements into a cohesive whole," said WKND Lab.

Chimi Chair by Mokamjunamoo

Design studio Mokamjunamoo presented Chimi Chair at the exhibition. It was informed by chimi, a sculptural element found at the ends of the ridge lines in traditional Korean wooden architecture.

"Chimi Chair functions both as a utilitarian object and as an exploration of how the sculptural language of traditional architecture can be translated into a contemporary, everyday context," said Mokamjunamoo founder of Hwan Tae Kim.

Drawing in Space, by Cheon Woosun

Metal artist Cheon Woosun created vessel-like forms by welding metal wires with silver.

Drawing from the shape of Korean ceramic jars, the vessels were formed by connecting individual wires, which the Woosun described as "sketching in pencil".

Design Miami Seoul 2026 took place from 31 August to 6 September 2026 at Design Lab within Dongdaemun Design Plaza, Seoul, South Korea. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

The construction of a 250-foot-high triumphal arch in Washington DC designed by Atlanta-based Harrison Design, is set to begin "over the next two-week period".

Plans to begin construction of the giant arch, alongside the Arlington Memorial Bridge on the south bank of the Potomac River, were announced last week by US interior secretary Doug Burgum.

"We are pleased to announce that after a very long wait (over 125 years!), we are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the great triumphal arch and military observation deck, at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery," he wrote on X (formerly Twitter).

"This will be one of the Great Pieces of American architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful capital in the World."

Officially called the Triumphal Arch of Washington DC, the structure is one of numerous additions being made to the city by US president Donald Trump.

Nicknamed the "Arc de Trump" – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris – the arch will be nearly 100 feet (30 metres) taller than its Parisian counterpart.

The arch, which was approved by the US Commission of Fine Arts in May, was designed by Atlanta-based studio Harrison Design. It will be neoclassical in style and topped by three gilded angels.

Within the structure will be three floors of accessible space to allow the structure to be a visitor attraction.

Read:

"Arc de Trump" design approved for Washington DC

On the ground floor will be a space for ticketing and security, with spiral staircases and lifts giving access to the upper floors.

Four galleries for exhibitions, along with restrooms, will be located within the main attic space, with the open-air observation deck above.

The arch is one of several major construction projects led by Trump that are currently underway in the US capital city.

The most significant of which, the addition of a ballroom to the White House, is moving forward after the US Supreme Court ruled that construction can continue.

The imagery is by Harrison Design via CFA.

"Breccia Rosa captures this moment, bringing a warm colour into a complex form capable of interacting with and enhancing other materials within a space."

item.content:encoded:
A thousand tonnes of volcanic rock replace concrete and steel in Petra Heights, a housing development in north London by architecture studio Groupwork and engineer Webb Yates.

The apartment building at 317 Finchley Road consists of three blocks ranging from six to 10 storeys, all held up by an exoskeleton of unreinforced stone.

This ladder frame single-handedly carries the high-rise's weight and wind loads, with no concrete stability core or concrete columns, no steel reinforcement bars and no need for cladding since the stone acts as both structure and facade.

"All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone," said Webb Yates co-founder Steve Webb, who describes the solution as a "world-first". "If the stone wasn't here, it would be a pile of rubble," he added.

Made of Sicilian basalt and Norwegian larvikite, the frame's post-and-lintel construction follows the same logic as Groupwork and Webb Yates's controversial Stirling Prize-shortlisted 15 Clerkenwell Close.

While the previous building was shorter, at six-storeys, it still relied on a concrete core to steady it against the wind. Petra Heights eliminates this emissions-intensive building element entirely.

"It's really escalating an idea," Webb told Dezeen. "So Clerkwell is a load-bearing exoskeleton, Finchley Road is load bearing exoskeleton stability structure, and then if we build another one, it can be taller, higher, stronger."

The building represents the latest step in the studios' ongoing, 15-year mission to establish stone as a viable, low-carbon alternative for steel and concrete, which together account for 16 per cent of humanity's emissions.

Load-bearing stone is second only to carbon-sequestering timber in its sustainability, they argue, and can cut the embodied carbon footprint of a building's superstructure by up to 95 per cent if quarried in the same country.

"This is what any architect and engineer should be doing," Groupwork founder Amin Taha told Dezeen. "Start off with timber. Where can the timber not be used? Then the next material should be stone because it's so low in embodied carbon."

Crucially, stone can also go where mass timber can't, which according to UK fire regulations is any building above 18 metres.

The exoskeleton that holds up Petra Height, on the other hand, could be scaled up to build a 30-storey skyscraper, which could cut emissions by 80 per cent compared to a steel frame at no additional cost, research from Groupwork and Webb Yates suggests.

"Finchley Road is interesting in its own right, but it's more interesting because it's a kind of stepping stone to some bigger changes and a kind of demonstration project of what can be done," Webb explained.

Set on a tricky site between a train station and the six-lane artery of Finchley Road, Petra Heights still relies on concrete basement foundations and floor slabs, as well as imported stone.

But its carbon footprint from materials and construction remains around 32 per cent less than that of a comparable reinforced-concrete structure, the studios said.

Using a stone-and-timber flooring system – as the studios had originally planned – could've pushed the savings up to 75 per cent.

To limit transport emissions, the original aim was to build Petra Heights from local rock. But at the time of the project's inception, just three years after Clerkenwell Close, the duo struggled to find a UK quarry excavating large enough pieces of strong enough stone to create the building's 572 columns and beams, the largest of which is five metres long.

Instead, the team pivoted to Sicilian basalt, manually split and cut into shape by Italian stonemason Ateliers Romeo using a computerised diamond-wire saw and a spreadsheet breaking down the exact dimensions of every block.

As construction dragged on over the pandemic, that quarry, too, struggled to create bigger pieces, and the team switched to larvikite from Norway's Lundhs quarry – the company's first structural stone project for almost 100 years since supplying the columns for Oslo's public library in 1933.

Read:

Design Museum pushes for stone construction in the UK with Stone Demonstrator

"Probably today, if this came to the drawing board, we wouldn't make it in very large pieces of stone like that," Webb said. "We'd tension up smaller pieces because you don't have to find a special quarry with especially strong, large pieces of stone."

"You could actually use UK stone, piece it together in this country, so you don't have to transport it for long distances, and it's cheaper because you're not finding that special quarry," he continued.

Basalt was used for the building's lower storeys, while the larvikite can be seen on the upper storeys, the tallest of which reaches up to 30 metres above ground.

To unify these different volcanic rocks, Groupwork used a chemical wash to oxidise the stone and bring out its iron content. This is what gives the building its distinctive rusty colour, blending in with the area's historic red-brick homes.

Similar techniques have been used by stonemasons for generations in restoration projects to match freshly cut stone to the existing structure, according to Taha.

"It used to be called soot-washing, so you would get soot from a chimney and mix it and brush it across stone to make it look older," he said.

In total, the exoskeleton consists of more than 1,000 tonnes of stone, joined together using steel dowels and brackets plus some epoxy mortar.

To reduce the building's mass and maximise its awkwardly shaped site, the structure is split into three blocks that, between them, house 22 apartments plus a glass-fronted shop set behind a colonnade on the ground floor.

Groupwork also decided to chamfer back the top few storeys of all three blocks so they can't be seen from the surrounding conservation areas.

Petra Heights' upper storeys – and the roof gardens set atop the two shorter blocks – can be accessed via a lightweight open-air staircase and an elevator at the heart of the plan.

Made from prefabricated stone modules, dropped in one on top of the other, the lift shaft was erected in just a day and a half, in what Webb believes might be another world's first. An adjoining riser core, housing utilities and services, was constructed of 2,400 stone bricks.

"This has shown that an ordinary general contractor can very easily develop methodologies and procedures to build a stone structure without needing somebody who's done 50 years of apprenticeship carving the stone of Notre Dame or whatever," he said.

Taha and Webb argue that Petra Heights's load-bearing stone exoskelleton offers a "far more interesting, more sustainable, more ethical kind of architecture" than the brick-clad buildings that have come to dominate UK architecture in recent years, accounting for five of the six projects on this year's Stirling Prize shortlist.

They hope it can serve as a model for how the 1.5 million new homes the government has promised to deliver by 2029 could be built in a more sustainable way.

"Building a million homes in our vernacular housing typology, which is fake brick stuck on concrete frame, is an environmental catastrophe," Webb said.

"The impact of removing the concrete core from high rises, has a big carbon benefit," he continued. "And I think the applicability of that in the UK for all medium rise housing – get rid of all the brickwork, get rid of all the concrete cores from concrete medium rise housing – will put a big dent in the carbon footprint of the million homes."

In upcoming projects, including a recently greenlit development in Hackney, Groupwork and Webb Yates are already planning to bring down their use of steel and concrete even further.

The project, which Taha self-financed by selling his home and office in Clerkenwell Close, aims to go carbon negative by cutting out concrete almost entirely with the help of stone foundations and the stone-and-timber flooring system they had intended for Petra Heights.

The photography is by Tim Soar.

item.content:encoded:
Britain's design industry has grown by 40 per cent and is now responsible for £1 in every £20 generated across the country, according to a landmark report from the Design Council.

Published today, the report paints a positive picture of a thriving design industry, which contributed £136.7 billion in gross value added (GVA) to the UK economy in 2023 – a 40 per cent rise from 2019.

As a result, the design industry has overtaken the £114 billion retail sector as the single biggest contributor to the national economy, the report argues.

It is now almost twice the size of the £70 billion accommodation and food service industry, and responsible for around £1 in every £20 generated nationwide.

The sector has also outpaced the UK economy as a whole, which grew by only 24 per cent over the same period.

"80 per cent of designers work in other parts of the economy"

Ahead of the report's publication, the Design Council's chief design officer Cat Drew spoke to Dezeen about the findings.

"Design is an essential business capability across industries with designers operating across the whole of the economy, from urban planning to computer games," she said.

"We classify some designers as working in design industries, in businesses such as architecture firms or fashion houses, but 80 per cent of designers work in other parts of the economy," Drew added.

"For example, healthcare providers such as the NHS now have digital teams, and financial service providers rely on in-house designers to create new products and services."

The report also found that the design economy has seen a 15 per cent increase in employment since 2020 – adding around 297,000 jobs – and currently supports 2.27 million jobs.

During this period, total UK employment grew by less than 2.5 per cent, highlighting the comparative expansion of the design sector.

The Design Council also found that design-led growth is being felt beyond London and the southeast of the UK, regions historically afforded the most creative opportunities.

Since 2019, the council reported an 88 per cent increase in design's economic contribution in Wales, a 67 per cent increase in the northeast and a 32 per cent increase in Scotland.

AI could present a threat to future growth

While these results point to a thriving industry, Drew acknowledged that it "is possible that we have captured a peak in the trend", considering the potential impacts of artificial intelligence (AI).

"It's likely too early to see the effect of AI on the design workforce in the medium-term data trend, from 2020 to 2025, and when looking at the design economy as a whole," she said.

A survey from the World Economic Forum previously found that graphic design is considered one of the jobs most at risk from AI, while the demand for UX and UI designers is expected to grow.

Early indications in the Design Council report seem to reflect this trend.

"When we look more granularly, growth in graphic design slowed between 2023 and 2025," she continued. "Digital design by comparison has seen a boom, now accounting for 59 per cent of the whole design economy and growing by 26 per cent to over 1 million people employed."

"If you're 16 today, studying design isn't only training to become a graphic designer in a design studio," added Drew.

"It's developing the ability to understand people, frame problems, generate solutions and turn ideas into things that work and those capabilities require human sensibilities that AI cannot replace."

Design needs a "more diverse talent pipeline"

Drew also acknowledged AI as a possible threat to the next generation of designers, with automation chipping away at entry-level opportunities that traditionally help young people get a foot in the door.

Risks to the future skills pipeline also emerge earlier on in education, with 68 per cent fewer students taking the Design and Technology (D&T) GCSE course between 2014 and 2024, while the number of D&T teachers was halved.

Drew emphasised the sustained lack of sufficient progress towards workforce diversity as another key pillar of the report.

Read:

Big-name studios encouraging architects to use AI

"Our new findings show that only two per cent of designers were female in 2025 and only two per cent of designers were Black, compared to five per cent in the UK workforce," she said.

"We need to attract a more diverse talent pipeline if the products, services, buildings and public spaces they produce are to be truly inclusive and accessible."

Last year, the Design Council hosted the World Design Congress, which took place in London.

The biennial event included a keynote speech by architect Norman Foster on the importance of walkable cities, and another talk with musician Brian Eno, who emphasised the importance of communities in the design world.

The images are courtesy of the Design Council.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture collective Badweather has transformed a 17-metre canal boat into Soak, an off-grid bathhouse that moves to a new location along London's waterways every two weeks.

Soak combines a wood-fired sauna, two cold plunge pools, showers, changing facilities and a small bar for up to 12 people.

It operates without mains water, electricity or sewage connections, instead drawing water directly from the canal and passing it through a six-stage filtration and UV treatment system before it is used for bathing.

Electricity is generated by solar panels and stored in an onboard battery system, while a wood-fired stove provides heat for the sauna.

The project was developed by Badweather co-founder Leo Sixsmith and chef and former restaurateur Riccardo Codacci-Pisanelli, who wanted to create a communal bathing space that could move through the city rather than occupy a permanent site.

"The changing location of the boat means that the view through these windows is never the same," Sixsmith told Dezeen.

Soak began with a near-derelict 20-year-old canal boat, with rotten floors, water damage and a steel hull that required extensive restoration. Around 40 people worked on its conversion, with the existing hull dictating much of the interior layout.

The exterior was painted cream with black and red detailing, while circular portholes puncture the sides of the boat.

Read:

Future Simple Studio creates "contemporary vocabulary" for Montreal bathhouse

Inside, the original 11-inch openings have been enlarged to 18 and 32 inches, with fiery-red frames that make the windows stand out against the hull.

At the bow, a large picture window replaces an original steel door, opening the narrow interior towards the water.

The interior follows the boat's long, narrow form. Visitors enter through a dark changing and reception area lined with stained marine plywood. They then pass into a brighter plunge and shower room, featuring pale green tiles, stainless-steel pools and a central skylight that brings daylight into the boat.

"The wet room is intentionally kept completely free of timber," Sixsmith said. "Its harder, clinical finish allows for easier maintenance, while heightening the sensory contrast with the warmth of the sauna."

At the bow, the sauna is lined with thermally treated Aspen and Alder wood and is centred around a wood-burning stove.

Two benches were suspended from aluminium beams rather than supported by legs, allowing them to overlap within the tapered hull.

The boat's cramped dimensions were a major constraint, but Badweather aimed to use them to shape the interior. "Every centimetre had to work exceptionally hard," Sixsmith said.

Founded in London in 2019 by Oli Brenner, Sophie Mei Birkin and Sixsmith, Badweather is an experimental architecture, scenography and design collective working across installations, objects, lighting and buildings.

Its previous work includes temporary structures for nightclubs and festivals, including the ongoing Pipeline project, a floating communal hearth made from reused corrugated polycarbonate.

Other bathhouses featured on Dezeen include a communal sauna and hydrotherapy bathhouse in Montreal and the turquoise-tiled Komaeyu public bathhouse in the suburbs of Tokyo.

The photography is by Kaye Song.

item.content:encoded:
Royal College of Art graduate Oliver Stiff has created a series of sculptural furniture pieces that aim to "bring the language, attitude and materials of fashion design into furniture".

The London-based designer's recent works include the Hurmull Chair and Side Table set, alongside the Socialite Chair, which was made using deadstock fabrics donated by global fashion house Vivienne Westwood.

"Fashion understands how to create desire and identity through styling, image-making and storytelling. I think furniture can operate in that same way," Stiff told Dezeen.

"I use bodily reference, silhouette, material and the idea of dressing an object to create pieces that feel provocative and culturally charged, almost as though the furniture itself has a character."

The Hurmull Chair and Side Table were hand-crafted using recycled tubular steel that was welded into shape and covered using sustainably sourced leather offcuts.

Informed by corsetry, the leather was stretched and tensioned around the continuous stainless steel frames with laced detailing to mimic the function and aesthetic of the structured garment.

"I was looking closely at corsetry and the way a corset shapes and supports the body through tension," said Stiff. "The shape deliberately references the waist and hips, giving the chair an almost bodily silhouette."

"The Hurmull Side Table developed as a continuation of that same construction language, but in a much simpler form," he continued.

Meanwhile, the Socialite Chair combines FSC-certified birch plywood and recycled metal to form its curvaceous, low-seated frame.

Deadstock textiles sourced from designer Vivienne Westwood were used to create the patchwork upholstery and the chair was then styled alongside a model wearing garments from the fashion house's latest collection.

Read:

Dezeen's favourite furniture and lighting from August

"I didn't know exactly what materials I would receive, so there was an element of designing with unpredictability," said Stiff. "The diﬀerent fabrics, patterns and scales had to be composed across the chair almost like styling an outfit or constructing a patchwork garment."

"For the final imagery, Andreas Kronthaler provided garments from Vivienne Westwood's latest collection to style the shoot, allowing the fashion and the furniture to exist within the same visual world," he added.

The Socialite Chair was designed to question where value is placed on high-end fashion textiles once they are not associated with the industry. By repurposing surplus materials, Stiff hoped to show that the value of these materials extends beyond the original use.

"These are incredibly high quality materials – including Italian textiles from manufacturers such as Tessilbiella – yet an offcut can go from being considered luxury to waste simply because it is no longer required for production," said Stiff.

"It made me question what we actually define as waste and where the value of a luxury material really sits."

Stiff explained that while sustainability was central to his design process, he wanted to create pieces that still felt theatrical, glamorous and visually distinctive.

"I'm interested in challenging the idea that sustainable design has to have a particular aesthetic, that it needs to look recycled, modest and restrained in order to communicate that it is responsible," he said.

Stiff was awarded the Ultrafabrics Sustainable Design Award for forward-thinking creatives at this year's edition of New Designers held in London.

item.content:encoded:
The sandy tones of Belgium's North Sea shore informed the interiors of this penthouse, designed by Antwerp-based studio Merckx-Holvoet Architecten.

The holiday home, named V Penthouse, occupies the ninth and tenth floors of a building in Duinbergen, a seaside village in the West Flanders region of Belgium.

"[We] aimed for an interior that envelops without overwhelming, one that reveals itself slowly rather than all at once," Merckx-Holvoet Architecten co-founders Marc Merckx and Sebastien Holvoet told Dezeen.

"The design centres on poetry and refinement, built around a reduced palette of materials and colours," the architects continued.

Merckx-Holvoet Architecten filled the 150-square-metre penthouse with a pared-back material palette and neutral tones that echo the dunes of the beach it overlooks.

"The starting point was the sand colour found along the coastline," project architect Jef De Saedeleer said. "Where the view stretches out over the sea, the material palette echoes this seamlessly."

Throughout the residence, walls covered in sandblasted Travertino Noce stone are teamed with lime-based flooring and solid oakwood details.

Across both floors, the penthouse follows a simple, rectangular layout, with an entrance foyer at the centre of the lower floor where Merckx-Holvoet Architecten installed a sculptural, solid oak staircase leading upstairs.

The foyer is flanked by a sea-view living room on one side and a kitchen-cum-dining area on the other – both opening into a verandah.

The studio chose neutral-hued furnishings for the living room, which it paired with tactile, modernist furniture pieces including a coffee table clad in parchment leather.

Read:

Woonpioniers builds a house that "moves with the dunes"

Floor-to-ceiling Travertino Noce shutters conceal built-in worktops and storage in the kitchen, complemented by an oak wood island topped with a chamfered block of Egyptian sandstone.

Merckx-Holvoet Architecten custom-made an Italian lavastone-topped table and an L-shaped bench crafted with Egyptian sandstone and oak wood for the dining area. The studio also sourced woven dining chairs for this space.

The homogeneous material palette continues in the primary bedroom and guest suites located upstairs.

The primary bedroom features an ensuite topped with a sloping roof. Here, Merckx-Holvoet Architecten installed picture windows by the bathtub as well as the shower area, both providing endless views of the North Sea.

Much of the furniture and lighting was custom-made by Merckx-Holvoet Architecten, including a mahogany table lamp and an outdoor aluminium stool for the verandah.

Minimalist artwork is dotted across the walls, including pieces by artists Andy Warhol and Sol Lewitt.

Merckx-Holvoet Architecten is an architecture and design practice founded in 2018 by Merckx and Holvoet.

Elsewhere in Belgium, Atelier Vens Vanbelle referenced brick industrial buildings to create a family home and Studio Okami Architecten extended a residence by adding a pavilion-like volume clad in green marble.

The photography is by Eric Petschek.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: hand-painted silk clothing inspired by robins is among the projects from Häme University of Applied Sciences.

Also featured is a fashion collection that takes its shape from architect Alvar Aalto's work and a dress made from recycled jeans.

Häme University of Applied Sciences

Course: Smart and Sustainable Design

School statement:

"Häme University of Applied Sciences (HAMK) is shaping the next generation of material‑driven designers in our Smart and Sustainable Design bachelor's degree programme, where forward‑looking experimentation, craft heritage and contemporary design thinking meet.

"Rooted in Finland's long tradition of material innovation, our programme encourages students to push the boundaries of form, technique and sustainable making.

"This selection presents emerging designers and their work from our fashion programme. It showcases a wide range of approaches within the discipline, from traditional handcraft and material manipulation and experimentation, to functional fashion design and innovative, forward-thinking approaches.

"Each project expresses a unique design voice and demonstrates a strong interest in exploring new directions in fashion through sustainability and new technology.

"Supported by dedicated fashion design studios and a wide range of materials, tools and technologies for experimentation, our emerging designers are guided by experienced staff as they develop, prototype and produce their own fashion designs.

"Through practical making and innovative design processes, they are empowered to become creative changemakers and contribute to a more sustainable future for fashion."

The Light of Silhouettes by Elsa Babkova

"The collection is an embrace of complexity within simplicity, inspired by how light forms silhouettes of buildings and defines its spotlight.

"Here, light is translated into lines. A silver and gold gradient that moves from dense areas to gradually wider spacing. The lines create a pattern that runs across the front, side and back of the garments.

"A specific sewing system was developed for the skirt. It involved extensive testing to find the right threads, colours and attachment methods. In total, the process took more than 400 hours of work.

"The skirt can also be worn in different orientations, allowing either the silver or gold side to be positioned at the front or the back.

"This creates a shifting visual composition and adds transformability to the piece, changing its appearance depending on how it is worn."

Student: Elsa Babkova
Course: Collaboration Project 3
Email: elzababkova[at]gmail.com

Oodi Collection, Kajo (shirt) and Halla (skirt) by Marjo Nieminen

"The Kajo shirt is a reversible woven half-sleeve shirt paired with the Halla skirt, a long A-line woven skirt, both made from vibrant taffeta.

"Both are part of the Oodi collection, inspired by Alvar Aalto's architecture and object design. The collection captures forms and lines from his design, transforming them into garments.

"Designed for women who appreciate clarity, comfort and versatility, the Oodi collection is created using zero waste methods and monomaterial for recyclability.

"The footwear in the photo is by Lauri Leino."

Student: Marjo Nieminen
Course: Collaboration Project 3
Email: marjo.nieminen[at]student.hamk.fi

Shifting Sands Collection by Roosa Lundström

"Shifting Sands is a 3D garment collection developed entirely in VStitcher. It draws inspiration from the natural patterns and tones of sand and water. The process started with physical textile experiments and sketching.

"These were translated into digital garments by building patterns, creating custom 3D fabrics and testing material behaviour.

"Hand-dyed textiles and crochet samples were digitised through pattern repeats and fabric scanning.

"Working in 3D made it possible to adjust fit, proportion and surface in real time, reducing the need for physical samples while supporting an iterative design process."

Student: Roosa Lundström
Course: Collaboration Project 3
Email: roosa.lundstrom[at]gmail.com

Fragments of Blue Denim Dress by Serine Turan

"The product is a long dress made from old denim jeans. The design combines layering, raw edges, and vertical forms that create movement and depth.

"The garment has an unfinished aesthetic while emphasising the reuse of materials and a unique, personal style. The footwear in the photo is by Senja Kaukonen."

Student: Serine Turan
Course: Basics of Fashion 1
Email: serineadla[at]gmail.com

Emerging Spring by Saara Kaarla

"This outfit was developed as part of a project-course. The research focused on the use of glass in fashion, exploring both glass-based elements and ways to recreate the material's transparency and texture through natural fibres.

"Inspired by Tiffany stained glass and traditional lamp-making techniques, I experimented with cotton organza to capture the qualities of glass while maintaining a natural-material approach.

"The collection, Emerging Spring, reflects the transition from winter to spring, drawing inspiration from melting ice and the first signs of awakening nature.

"The designs express a sense of transparency, lightness and anticipation of the season to come. The footwear in the photo is by Selma Repo."

Student: Saara Kaarla
Course: Multidisciplinary Project
Email: saara.kaarla[at]gmail.com

Närästys by Jing Yu

"Närästys is a wearable art piece crafted from discarded plastic bags. It is inspired by the burning sensation of heartburn and the visual chaos of erupting volcanoes.

"The sculptural silhouette echoes pulsating blood vessels, combining organic texture with dramatic form. Plastic waste is cut, layered and heat-shaped using a heat gun.

"As a result, refused material is transformed into an expressive red-carpet garment. This work challenges fast fashion's environmental destruction by revealing the aesthetic potential of waste.

"It merges my passion for design with a commitment to sustainability, provoking a critical rethinking of how we create and consume fashion – proving that even discarded materials can become emotionally powerful and visually stunning.

"The footwear in the photo is by Jing Yu."

Student: Jing Yu
Course: Thesis Project
Email: jjfish0122[at]gmail.com

Knitwear Collection by Roosa Siirtola

"This collection was created using surplus production materials. The aim was to research the possibilities of reusing yarn materials for knitwear and view the interpretation of various knitwear surfaces through garments.

"There were two collections. The first collection's inspiration was based on Space, more specifically the surface of the moon. The second collection focused on organic textures, such as skin folds and the surfaces of moon rocks.

"These elements can be seen as three-dimensional structures in the knitwear.

"The sustainable perspective to the design process was based on the idea of exploring reused materials and finding new ways to give them new forms. The knitwear collections were produced using knitting machines."

Student: Roosa Siirtola
Course: Collaboration Project 3
Email: roosa[at]siirtola.fi

Timeless Threads by Laura Jukola, Milda Ramanauskiene, Jing Yu, Annika Koivula, Heli Sahanen and Olga Saukonoja

"The assignment was to design unisex workwear for artists and designers. The outfit consists of a structured blazer, relaxed fit trousers, and a belt bag with a pouch.

"This workwear outfit allows the wearer to blur the lines between feminine and masculine. Each piece was made from recycled textile leftovers.

"The textiles were dyed tone-on-tone to give the impression of artistic spirit. As a result, the textiles have a new purpose as a stunning workwear set.

"We also aimed to create a jacket that would replace a bag as a fitting solution. Through our research, we concluded that designers' need for workwear depends on the occasion.

"We wanted to tackle another aspect of working life  – one where a designer's tools are specifically designed to be easily portable."

Students: Laura Jukola, Milda Ramanauskiene, Jing Yu, Annika Koivula, Heli Sahanen and Olga Saukonoja
Course: Collaboration Project 2

Robin Collection by Mari Heiskanen and Susanna Hyvärinen

"The Robin collection celebrates craftsmanship and blurs the boundaries between contemporary fashion, art and costume design.

"At its core is the robin bird: a symbol, rooted in folklore, of a messenger between the living and those who have passed.

"The collection embodies a balance of strength and fragility, designed to evoke deep emotions. The primary materials are vivid dupion silk and delicate silk-cotton blends.

"Each garment in the collection is a unique work of art. The luxurious fabrics are hand-painted or dyed in small, intricate patches, and every piece is made to order."

Students: Mari Heiskanen and Susanna Hyvärinen
Course: Collaboration Project 3
Email: s.hyvarinen[at]outlook.com

item.content:encoded:
UK studio Hudson Architects has converted a disused commercial building in Norfolk into a public library, wrapping its existing concrete structure in a skin of cement shingles.

Named King's Lynn Library, the project adapted the neglected structure of a former nightclub, car park and retail store into a more central home for the local library, which was underused due to its location on the town's outskirts.

A key aspect of Hudson Architects' approach was to reduce the size of the existing concrete structure to echo the scale of the neighbouring buildings, freeing up space to create an expanded public street at its entrance.

"A major element of our role was to turn the building's rather lumpen presence into something more attractive, welcoming and better attuned to its location on the edge of a conservation area and the town's modern shopping district," studio director Louise Boddie told Dezeen.

"So much of the building's success arises from the early decision to retain as much of the original building as possible," she added.

Modifications to the existing structure included carving out a large skylit atrium out of its centre and cutting the southern corner to address the street with a glazed frontage.

Inside, the concrete structure of King's Lynn Library is left exposed to frame the interiors, softened by a zigzagging timber stair and panelled walls.

Meanwhile, externally, it has been clad in cement shingles with a pale colour palette that references the tones of the neighbouring buildings.

"Despite its dramatic transformation, it is not immediately obvious to visitors that this is an older, reused building," Boddie said.

"The building's history, including all its dents and marks, reveals itself slowly, and we think that is part of the joy of experiencing it," she continued. "Different shades of cement shingles to create a mottled and varied effect across the facade, echoing the tones and textures of nearby buildings."

Read:

Demountable timber library in Amsterdam is "a living room for the neighbourhood"

On the ground floor, a children's library has been given a castle theme that nods to the medieval town centre, with arched and crenellated play structures and shelving beneath a ceiling of wavy timber acoustic baffles.

Above, the first floor contains open reading areas, with long desks positioned around the edge of the central atrium, and staff spaces at the perimeter alongside an additional stair and lift that ensure the library is fully accessible.

The more enclosed second floor contains a series of educational rooms including a training kitchen, positioned to overlook the city through rows of large square windows.

Previous projects by Hudson Architects include a low-carbon home in Norfolk that was built using cob – an unfired earth-based construction material consisting of clay-rich earth, water and fibrous material such as straw.

Other libraries recently featured on Dezeen include a demountable timber structure designed as "a living room" for Amsterdam and one in Luanda that winds around existing trees on its site.

The photography is by Fred Howarth.

Blue-stained plywood and knotted larch feature in our latest lookbook of residential interiors anchored by statement wooden staircases.

There is no end to architects' appetite for building with wood, with recent wooden projects around the world ranging from a demountable library in Amsterdam to a cedar and hempcrete chicken coop in Portugal.

The following homes also make the most of the material in their interior designs, which are defined by wooden staircases in various formations.

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring colourful taps, scenic bathrooms and striking patios.

Cobalt Coach House, UK, by Foils

A plywood staircase forms the centrepiece of this southeast London home, tinted in a cobalt blue stain to reveal its swirly grain.

British architecture studio Foils renovated the former coach house in Peckham to create more space, which included the addition of the bespoke stair that was constructed in five parts and assembled on site.

Find out more about Cobalt Coach House ›

Wooden Annex, Mexico, by Pedro & Juana

Wooden Annex is a Mexican house extension in Valle de Bravo, which was conceived from two steel U-beams and a dried pine tree.

The interior of the staircase was also lined with pine and punched with porthole-style windows.

"You can say [that the project] served as a laboratory to prove that designing with wood in Mexico is possible, beautiful, and a more sustainable answer than the omnipresent construction with everything concrete," said architecture studio Pedro & Juana.

Find out more about Wooden Annex ›

London house, UK, by Waind Gohil and Potter Architects

Fabricated offsite and assembled like a puzzle, this boxy wooden staircase defines a small dwelling in the garden of a Shepherd's Bush home in west London.

The staircase connects all three levels of the property and was constructed entirely from an engineered-timber product with a knotted larch finish.

Find out more about this London house ›

Barn at the Ahof, the Netherlands, by Julia van Beuningen

Dutch Architectural designer Julia van Beuningen renovated this 19th-century barn in Gelderland to create a rental home with four bedrooms and a large open-plan living space.

The centrepiece of the living space is a strikingly spiralled plywood staircase, characterised by a curved geometry that offers a playful contrast to the barn's traditional wooden columns and beams.

Find out more about Barn at the Ahof ›

Light House, Croatia, by OFIS Arhitekti 

Light House is an unusual stone property on the Croatian island of Cres, which was renovated with a slatted timber framework throughout that acts as furniture and allows daylight to filter through the entire interior.

Slovenian studio OFIS Arhitekti incorporated a staircase into the striking framework, fluidly connecting the dwelling's three storeys.

Find out more about Light House ›

Casa Thomé Beira da Silva, Brazil, by Marcos Bertoldi Arquitetos

A monolithic helical staircase sits at the heart of Casa Thomé Beira da Silva, a Curitiba home by local firm Marcos Bertoldi Arquitetos.

Crafted from timber, the stepped structure is flanked by latticed wooden screens that filter daylight into the open-plan interior.

Find out more about Casa Thomé Beira da Silva ›

The Arbor House, Scotland, by Brown & Brown

Scottish architecture studio Brown & Brown married stone salvaged from a dilapidated farmstead with wood and board-marked concrete to bring The Arbor House to life.

Located in a conservation area in Aberdeen, the house has a dining and circulation space with a tightly twisted birch plywood staircase.

"The stair was assembled over three weeks as timber treads were individually cut and hand-layered to form a smooth, sinuous parabolic curve," said Brown & Brown.

Find out more about The Arbor House ›

London house, UK, by Paolo Cossu Architects

An extra-wide staircase designed to give residents a place to sit, chat or read features in this east London home by local studio Paolo Cossu Architects.

Crafted from chunky wooden blocks, the stair is connected to matching oak bookshelves that cover the adjacent wall.

item.content:encoded:
Architect Kristijan Markoc has created a downloadable template for a "deliberately modest", two-bedroom timber home designed to be adapted to any site.

Named Plana House, the replicable home design has a compact, 42-square-metre plan and is composed of a simple, pitched-roof structure that can be constructed using readily-available materials.

The home was designed by Markoc, who is founder of Swiss studio Plana Architecture, to be a more-accessible alternative to typical housing designs, prioritising affordability, adaptability and a straight-forward construction process.

Central to this idea was bringing residents back into the process of building a home, leading to Markoc's creation of freely-available technical drawing sets for the project.

Resource for people to "adapt and potentially build their own house"

"Traditionally, much of the knowledge needed to build a house was held in common by the people and communities who built and inhabited them," Markoc told Dezeen.

"Plana House seeks to place some of that knowledge back in the commons by making a complete set of architectural drawings freely available, so that people can use it as a resource to understand, adapt and potentially build their own house."

Markoc, who has plans to build a prototype of Plana House, drew on his knowledge of modular construction for the structure, which he designed in line with UK and Irish construction regulations.

Although the structure is adaptable, any construction of Plana House would still need to be reviewed by a licensed architect or qualified professional to meet local building regulations, Markoc explained.

"The house uses a simple timber frame based on a highly efficient structural grid, developed using my experience with modular construction methods to make the building as efficient and economical as possible," Markoc explained.

"All dimensions, details, and construction methods must be verified and adapted by a licensed architect or qualified professional to ensure compliance with local building regulations, site conditions, and applicable standards prior to construction," he added.

Renders of the design by Markoc showcase a simple, single-storey timber frame clad entirely with timber panels, which can be built from standard, off-the-shelf materials.

Externally, the structure is intended to be finished in a variety of materials depending on what is locally available. For flexibility, the home can be built atop screw piles or pad foundations for a light-touch approach.

Read:

Woonpioniers models adjoining Dutch homes on "a game of Tetris"

"[The structure] relies on readily available materials that can be purchased in any local hardware store, while its simple and familiar form allows it to sit naturally within very different regional contexts, with cladding materials adapted according to the local climate, availability and budget," Markoc said.

Inside, the home's rectangular plan is split into two wings, containing an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area at one end, and two bedrooms and a bathroom at the other.

A series of windows draw light into the interior, where the pitched roof helps to create more-spacious feel within the four-metre-wide spaces.

Elsewhere, Woonpioniers completed a pair of interlocking houses for two families within a single gabled volume in Utrecht.

The renders are by Tom Stepins.
