Also featured are woven shoes with 3D-printed soles and shoes made from tanned vegetable leather.

Häme University of Applied Sciences

Course: Smart and Sustainable Design Bachelor's degree

School statement:

"Häme University of Applied Sciences (HAMK) is shaping the next generation of material‑driven designers in our Smart and Sustainable Design Bachelor's degree programme, where forward‑looking experimentation, craft heritage and contemporary design thinking meet.

"Rooted in Finland's long tradition of material innovation, our programme encourages students to push the boundaries of form, technique and sustainable making.

"This selection presents emerging designers and their work from our footwear programme, showcasing a wide range of approaches within the discipline – from traditional handcraft and material investigation to functional footwear and forward-thinking modular design.

"Häme University of Applied Sciences (HAMK) is the only university in the Nordic countries where you can study footwear design.

"Each project expresses a unique design voice and demonstrates a strong interest in exploring new directions in footwear through sustainability, technology and upcycling.

"Supported by dedicated footwear design studios, a variety of materials, tools and technologies for experimentation, our emerging designers are guided by experienced staff as they develop, prototype and produce their own footwear.

"Through practical making and innovative design processes, they are empowered to become creative changemakers and help shape a more sustainable future for footwear."

Cult of Craft: Louise by Heidi Kannisto

"Louise shoes bring together the dimensions of traditional weaving and contemporary 3D modelling. The design process combines a creative, ragged upper with a meticulously refined sole built through 3D modelling.

"The shoe's exterior is playful and draws inspiration from late-90s pop culture as well as the design language of traditional, colourful rag rugs designed from upcycled materials.

"The shoe is designed to be glue-free and versatile. The upper can be attached to the sole in various ways, and at the end of its lifespan, it can be taken apart and the parts recycled properly."

Student: Heidi Kannisto
Course: Footwear Design and Development Bootcamp
Email: kannistoheidi[at]email.com

Mod by Lauri Leino, Sittichok Moungmee, Riko Kuokkanen, Miia Lilli and Georg Lichtenberg

"Traditional footwear design often leads to excessive waste, as worn-out or damaged shoes are frequently discarded rather than repaired.

"To rethink traditional footwear waste, we developed a modular shoe to combat the waste generated by the footwear industry, where millions of shoes end up in landfills each year due to reparable wear or fast fashion trends.

"By designing shoes with interchangeable and replaceable parts, we sought to create a more sustainable alternative that allows consumers to repair or customise their footwear instead of discarding it entirely."

Students: Lauri Leino, Sittichok Moungmee, Riko Kuokkanen, Miia Lilli and Georg Lichtenberg
Course: Emil Aaltonen Museum Collaboration Project

BarbieBoon by Selma Repo

item.content:encoded:
Canada's Ivy Studio has transformed a 1970s bank into a veterinary clinic for exotic animals in Laval, Quebec, featuring minimalist interiors and soft lighting.

The Fauna clinic occupies a standalone structure completed in a brutalist style near the waterfront, just over the Prairies River northwest of Montreal.

Ivy Studio leaned into the building's existing style to inform the interiors, creating a calm, minimalist environment for the patients and their handlers.

"By celebrating its historical shell, Fauna establishes a unique dialogue between imposing institutional architecture and the compassionate, soothing nature of veterinary care," the studio said.

The building spans 380 square metres over two levels, with the public areas and treatment facilities housed across the ground floor.

Boasting 16-foot (4.9-metre) ceilings, the reception and waiting areas maximise natural light from the building's existing windows.

The original concrete coffered ceiling is left exposed and painted a deep brown, contrasting concrete flooring and the warm grey of the textured plaster walls.

Facing the waiting area, the four consultation rooms are arranged in an offset row through the centre of the plan.

Each is faced with a curved wall that sweeps up to the tall ceiling, mimicking the building's exterior, and is also denoted by vertical partitions with stepped end-profile details.

"This dramatic gesture provides intimacy for the consultation rooms while serving as a sculptural focal point from the waiting area," said Ivy Studio.

Fluted glass doors slide open to access the consultation rooms, which feature walnut desks with chrome bases, matching the waiting room benches and the reception counter.

The individual rooms all link to the treatment area behind, where a spiral staircase leads down to office, storage and research space in the basement.

Read:

Ivy Studio converts historic bank building into offices for Montreal ad agency

Careful consideration was given to the lighting design, comprising diffused light boxes inside the consultation rooms along with the natural illumination in the other public spaces.

"A soothing environment is paramount for an exotic animal clinic, where patients are easily stressed," Ivy Studio said. "The lighting strategy in the public zones is soft, dimmed, and strictly indirect."

In the treatment room and basement, the building's concrete bones are exposed, and the fluted concrete walls are painted soft cream.

The bank's original vault is repurposed as a closed pharmacy and lab – the finishing touch in adapting the former financial institution into a contemporary medical facility.

Ivy Studio is perhaps best known for its hospitality projects across Canada, with completed restaurant projects ranging in style from Japanese minimalism to colourfully retro and bold and glamorous.

The studio's commercial portfolio includes a dry cleaners modelled on a Parisian apartment, an all-black spinning studio and offices for a digital advertising agency also housed in a former bank.

The photography is by Alex Lesage.

item.content:encoded:
A cluster of monolithic forms lined with grey brick and built into a steep bank defines Tollymore, a riverside house in Northern Ireland by Belfast studio McGonigle McGrath.

Located off a narrow road in County Down, Tollymore comprises six rectangular forms set at different levels across its steep site, which the studio said helps to "make it part of the landscape".

According to McGonigle McGrath, this design is a direct result of a "well-developed brief" set out by the client, in which they imagined a home divided into small "pods" that maximise views of nature and sounds of the adjacent river.

"It was a unique brief and a fantastic site, and between that and the client's enthusiasm at a particularly creative time in the practice, this design emerged as a new way of making spaces," studio principal Kieran McGonigle told Dezeen.

Each of Tollymore's volumes is raised on a stepped plinth formed from board-marked concrete. As they cascade down the sloped site, the roofline is at the same level, meaning the volumes differ in scale.

Between them are walkways, covered passages and courtyards, giving rise to an arrangement intended to evoke water flowing around the stones in the river.

The six blocks include two living areas, three sleeping zones and one that can be used as either.

Moving between the bedrooms and living spaces brings the family briefly outside, which is "a ritual experience of the views and sounds of the river, mountains and sky, whatever the weather", said the studio.

While each volume has a unique function, they were all designed to be flexible to adapt to the family's changing needs and ensure usability well into the future.

"When the children are at college, and the block that is currently an Airbnb let is not being used, the clients can close down three of the six blocks, significantly increasing the running costs of the building," said McGonigle.

Read:

Arquitecturia designs Catalan house as cluster of pavilions around garden

Tollymore's monolithic structures are clad in grey brick walls and granite-gravel roofs, which, combined with the board-marked concrete plinths, are intended to evoke boulders.

"The material choices reinforce a sense of belonging by grounding the site within its place," explained McGonigle.

Inside, the interiors contrast the rock-like exterior with warm hardwoods and exposed wooden beams, alongside terrazzo and lime-washed plaster details.

Windows are also framed in hardwood, helping to establish a "transition to the warm interior". These also maximise outward views, either to the outdoors or other rooms.

McGonigle McGrath was founded by McGonigle with Aidan McGrath in 2012. In 2019, its project House Lessans in rural Northern Ireland won RIBA House of the Year.

Another house by the studio is Hill House, a similarly monolithic home that draws on the shapes and colours of local masonry buildings in Belfast.

The photography is by Johan Dehlin.

item.content:encoded:
With artificial intelligence encroaching on more and more aspects of daily life, there is a rising trend of fatigue and cynicism around the technology. Here, we round up five designs that push back on the AI boom.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked headlines around the world for its controversial use in mass video surveillance, data scraping and deepfake scams. In response, designers are coming up with innovative ways to protect people from some of the more sinister sides of AI.

While some of the designs may have been developed to encourage conversation around uses of AI, the increasing advancement of the technology might make them highly sought-after designs in the near future.

Digital Camouflage by Simon Weckert 

Designer Simon Weckert created a colourful patterned shirt that acts as camouflage against AI video systems by subverting what they recognise as a person.

The Digital Camouflage shirt was developed in response to a pilot project to use AI video surveillance at Berlin's Kottbusser Tor station, providing a way for its wearer to be undetectable. Its bold patterns were developed using an AI trial-and-error workflow known as an "adversarial loop".

"This was necessary because a machine's blind spots are not intuitive to humans; you cannot design against machine perception by eye, only the machine can tell you what it fails to see," said Weckert.

Find out more about Digital Camouflage ›

Quartz by Modem and Retinaa

Quartz is a concept for a ring that acts as a human identity verification method, developed by design studios Modem and Retinaa to counteract scammers using AI deepfakes to impersonate people.

In the design, two people bring their Quartz rings to touch in a handshake, establishing an encrypted bond that proves their identity when they later interact online or over the phone.

The Quartz concept incorporates technologies that exist today – finger-vein biometrics to identify the wearer, near-field communication to create a connection between rings, and cryptography to later confirm both parties' identities during remote interactions – but would need to be miniaturised and power-optimised to fit into a wearable ring.

Find out more about Quartz ›

Decoy Font by Mixfont

Optical illusion is at play in Decoy Font, which displays two overlapping messages readable by humans, while AI chatbots and large language models such as ChatGPT can only read one.

The font was designed by the company Mixfont for people who want to avoid having their data scraped and as a conversation starter concerning issues of AI and public trust.

"It started as an exploration of how AI and typography intersect, but it was also meant to raise awareness of the growing reach and capabilities of AI," Mixfont founder Eric Lu told Dezeen. "I think the reaction to the font shows that there are many folks who feel strong AI fatigue, and want a way to defend themselves against the presence of AI in their lives."

Find out more about Decoy Font ›

Manifesto Collection by Cap_able

Created by Italian fashion start-up Cap_able, Manifesto Collection is a series of knitted clothes adorned in colourful patterns designed to deceive facial recognition software in real-time.

Tested using the YOLO object detection system, people wearing Manifesto Collection jumpers, t-shirts, trousers and dresses were either undetectable by the AI software or identified as animals whose patterns feature on the clothing, such as dogs, zebras, or giraffes.

"In a world where data is the new oil, Cap_able addresses the issue of privacy, opening the discussion on the importance of protecting against the misuse of biometric recognition cameras: a problem if neglected, could freeze the rights of the individual, including freedom of expression, association and free movement in public spaces," Cap_able co-founder Rachele Didero told Dezeen.

Find out more about Manifesto Collection ›

Incognito by Ewa Nowak

Another wearable item designed in protest of facial recognition technology is Incognito, a mask designed by Polish designer Ewa Nowak to make the wearer's face unrecognisable to cameras and AI systems, as well as an aesthetic piece of facial jewellery.

Comprising geometric brass shapes fixed to a long wire moulded to the contours of the face, Nowak created the mask in an effort to reclaim the anonymity that they feel has been lost to face-detecting cameras installed in public spaces.

"Cameras are able to recognise our age, mood, or sex and precisely match us to the database – the concept of disappearing in the crowd ceases to exist," said Nowak. "This has a huge value in the form of increased security and detection of dangerous units. On the other hand, in which direction will the surveillance of society develop?"

Find out more about Incognito ›

item.content:encoded:
New York studio Surrane Design has outfitted Thai restaurant Hommali in New York with a terracotta floor, a central "courtyard" space and personal items of the founders to create a space that resembles a traditional Thai house.

Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives chef Chattchakorn "Benz" Khajornchaisan,  general manager Kritayanee "Air" Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak "Picha" Srigungvarl after they moved to New York City and met in the hospitality scene.

The restaurant contains an eight-seat bar, a 20-seat dining den, a semi-private mezzanine and auxiliary spaces such as a wine room and dry-age room where ducks and other ferments are on display.

Surrane Design layered the space with a rich assortment of textures and patterns, such as dark wood millwork, a marbled bar top and artwork sourced from Bangkok's Chatuchak Weekend Market.

According to the team, its palette of browns and greens was informed by the life cycle of a rice plant.

"The color palette is inspired by the stages of the rice plant: fresh green for young leaves, golden yellow for mature stalks, earthy brown for paddy soil, soft beige for rice husks, and warm cream white for polished rice," said the team.

It was designed to resemble a traditional Thai house, where the central dining den and mezzanine above recall a courtyard, and the terracotta floor also calls to the vernacular architecture of the country.

Visitors are greeted with a rice plant light installation at the doorway and enter by the bar, which is clad in a sandy fluted tile with seats upholstered in leather and velvet.

Two booths sit in front of the main dining space, which is tucked beneath the mezzanine. Curtains and open shelving separate the two spaces.

Personal items from the ownership team, such as vintage Thai cookbooks from the late 1960s and early 1970s and other objects "one would expect to find in a living room" line the shelves. Small bamboo sculptures by Thai artist Korakot Aromdee are also peppered throughout the space.

Read:

OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight"

Wood-lined stairs lead to the mezzanine above, which contains additional seating concealed behind a frosted glass railing. A large skylight hangs above the space and sits over a large dining table. Banquets and an off-white white wallpaper embossed with 3D-printed plants also line the space.

Like below, a curtain can be drawn across the length of the space to provide additional separation.

Hommali will serve contemporary takes on traditional Thai dishes created under Benz, such as a seafood cocktail with razor clams imbued with the hot and sour notes of tom yum and the Tomato, "a michelada-meets-spritz with a Singaporean rice wine base accompanied by a Thai chile tincture."

Surrane Design is an independent design studio based in Brooklyn by partners Bud Nitaya and Yoon Her.

Other recently opened spaces in the West Village include Love Thy Neighbour next to The Stonewall Inn and The Cherry Lane Theatre

item.content:encoded:
Skylit ceilings and zigzagging staircases animate this tall, skinny home and ceramics studio in Japan, completed by local studio Tato Architects.

Named House and Studio in Kyoto, the project was designed as a combined workspace and residence for a couple who are both ceramic artists.

Its distinctive form was the result of its challenging narrow plot, which measures four by 30 metres – a type of site known locally as an eel's bed.

With built-up neighbours to the north and the possibility of future development to the south, the biggest challenge for Tato Architects was access to daylight. This led to the creation of two skylit voids, informed by Kyoto's traditional townhouses or machiya.

"In a traditional machiya, the passage garden and small courtyards draw light and air deep into a long, narrow building," studio founder Yo Shimada told Dezeen.

"Here we raised that device into the vertical dimension, recomposing it as something that runs through all three storeys. It is these two voids that allow a deep, narrow, mid-rise building to work as both a place of production and a home," he added.

The voids of House and Studio in Kyoto serve not only to draw in light but also as vertical circulation cores that divide the home into two separate eastern and western wings above an expansive ground-floor studio.

At the heart of the building, the largest central void is crossed by zigzagging staircases and walkways that connect these two wings. Landings of fibre-reinforced plastic allow light through while reducing noise from the studio.

Both sides of the central void are lined with full-height walls of translucent glass, which help to illuminate both the ground-floor studio and the circulation spaces above.

"At 321 square metres, this is the largest newly built house our office has designed — but its use is not limited to a house," Shimada explained.

Read:

Tato Architects uses old barrels to clad exterior of home and shop

"The studio may also receive visitors from overseas, and we thought of the building as a place for creation and exhibition. In that sense it was designed at a scale closer to a public space than to a private residence," he added.

Facing the street to the west, an ensuite guest bedroom sits beneath a living, dining and kitchen area topped by a faceted timber ceiling, with slatted panels filtering through light from a skylight.

At the home's opposite end, an additional guest bedroom and study sit beneath the main bedroom, with small square cut-outs creating visual connections between these spaces and the central area.

Previous projects by Tato Architects include a home in Kyoto that also made use of skylights and silver-painted ceilings to maximise daylight on a constrained urban site, and a home and shop in Hofu that is clad in old barrels.

The photography is by Daici Ano.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture firm Studio Cadena has designed a forest-like interior for the Masa cafe in Medellín, Colombia, where over 30 plywood columns stretch to a concrete ceiling to create an "atmosphere without walls or enclosure".

For the design of the spacious cafe in Colombia's second largest city, the studio focused on two main materials: concrete and wood.

The eatery's main area, a six-metre-tall room where guests can enjoy Masa's coffees, smoothies and food, is defined by two large concrete slabs that appear to be held up by numerous slender columns.

However, the columns aren't load-bearing, but were introduced to create a striking interior that resembles a stylised forest.

"They do not carry the building; they carry the room," Studio Cadena said.

"Freed from load-bearing duty, they are multiplied across the interior to structure movement, filter light, and create a layered space, without the use of walls or partitions."

To Studio Cadena founder Benjamin Cadena, the repetitive design is what defines the architecture of the space.

"The concept was to shape the space's atmosphere without walls or enclosure," he told Dezeen.

"31 wooden columns sit within a six-metre-tall volume between two slabs. One move, repeated, does all the architectural work."

The architect carefully considered what material would have the most impact, landing on plywood due to its ability to subtly reflect the light in the space.

"Untreated pine-faced plywood was used to form the six-meter-tall columns," Cadena said. "Light bouncing off their surface is what gives the space its particular quality by introducing a diffused warmth."

Read:

Jagged windows pierce Studio Cadena's Masa bakery in Bogotá

His studio left the concrete structure exposed throughout the cafe to show the "raw shell" of the building, and refrained from adding too many materials to the pared-back space.

"Few materials were used," Cadena explained. "Wood, a marble counter, stainless steel for smaller pieces, with the structural shell left untouched."

"It was an intentional choice to be resourceful, and reflects a recurring interest in reducing the design to the essential elements that shape how the space will be used and felt over time," Cadena continued.

One side of the large room opens up towards a green outdoor space, with the wooden columns leading out towards the exterior to underline the connection to nature.

At the back of the room, a circular window gives visitors a view of the cafe's production area.

Throughout the space, Studio Cadena chose to let the materials speak for themselves, rather than using different colours.

"More than colour, the idea was contrast between the existing structure and what was introduced," Cadena said.

"Materials were left untreated, with more attention given to texture than hue. Colour enters the space indirectly, through natural materials, vegetation, and ultimately its occupants."

Other Medellín projects featured on Dezeen include a flat that "channels the 1980s" and a concrete office building on a steep hillsite.

item.content:encoded:
Finnish firm Elementic has unveiled MO6, a wall-surfacing material produced from forestry industry offcuts that is almost pure carbon.

Called MO6, the product takes the form of thick, lightweight tiles with a rough texture and an off-black colour.

Materials technology company Elementic established MO6 as a brand in May, with the debut collection, MO6 Eternal, launched on Wednesday at trade fair Habitare.

MO6 claims to be the most carbon-negative, or carbon-storing, building material in the world, with carbon molecules making up 90 per cent of its chemistry.

It uses lignin as a raw material – a by-product of the forestry and timber industry that is considered difficult to use and is usually burned for energy.

Through a patented process that remains highly secretive, impurities such as oxygen are removed from the lignin in a bioreactor to result in a material that is highly durable and fire-resistant with a dramatic aesthetic.

"It's quite a challenging material, but we love lignin because it's a very carbon-rich raw material," MO6 general manager Johanna Normiala told Dezeen.

"In our process, the know-how is all about knowing how you transform lignin to make it something useful," she continued.

"We take the lignin, we create a kind of dough that we bake like a cake, and in the end we get a hard, resistant, durable material but which is lightweight."

MO6, which describes itself as a "premium interior design brand", is already delivering product to projects, including a spa under construction in Paris.

"We are very much eager to help or support our customers whatever is the area of application, but I would say that the focused interest are in [the] area of hotels, restaurants – I think that's that's something where this material goes very well," said Normiala.

For the time being, MO6 is only being marketed as suitable for dry indoor spaces, but Elementic has ambitions for much wider applications and is currently developing bricks.

Read:

Tarkett achieves "world's first" carbon negative linoleum

"There's a huge potential for that, not only interior part, which is now our first business, but in future in a much larger scale in building," said Normiala.

MO6 Eternal tiles are available with a rougher or smoother finish, and can be coated.

According to Normiala, its thermal and acoustic properties are comparable to wood, but MO6 is hopeful that improvements can be made with tweaks to the manufacturing process in future.

Carbon negativity refers to something that removes more carbon dioxide equivalent from the atmosphere than it emits.

In the case of a material, emissions are generally produced during manufacture and end-of-life.

The issue of carbon storage has attracted major focus among architects in recent years, driven by concern about the vast carbon emissions associated with constructing buildings.

Read:

The Dezeen guide to carbon

Timber has been the subject of renewed interest as a building material as a result, thanks to the carbon sequestered by trees.

According to MO6, one kilogram of its material stores approximately 2.4 kilograms of atmospheric carbon dioxide – roughly double the amount stored by wood.

MO6 says its material can keep carbon locked up for potentially thousands of years, because it does not decay and is easy to recycle.

Dezeen previously explored innovations seeking to store and utilise atmospheric carbon through our Carbon revolution series.

Other projects published on Dezeen that aim to put lignin to use include a bioplastic developed by German designer Basse Stittgen and a structural panel by Denmark's Natural Material Studio.

The photography is courtesy of MO6.

item.content:encoded:
Following the unveiling of Dyson's CameraJet, the brand's Niamh Turney explained why it decided to redesign the toothbrush.

Revealed earlier this week, the Dyson CameraJet toothbrush includes a mouthwash jet directed by a camera to remove plaque between teeth.

According to Niamh Turney, senior commercial manager at Dyson, the brand made the move into dental hygiene as it aims to disrupt areas of technology that have not been developed for a long time.

"Every Dyson technology begins with identifying a problem that people have largely accepted and asking whether it can be solved differently," Turney told Dezeen.

"Dyson enters categories where there is a clear unmet need and where its engineering, software and fluid dynamics expertise can deliver a meaningful improvement in performance."

Dyson became a household brand after its founder, James Dyson, developed the bagless vacuum cleaner. Subsequently, the company has overhauled the design of other appliances including hand dryers, fans and heaters, while it recently unveiled its first headphones.

The brand viewed electric toothbrushes as another device that had not seen a major development leap for years.

"With oral care, we saw a routine that has remained largely unchanged for decades despite persistent challenges around flossing compliance and plaque removal between teeth," said Turney.

"Our ambition is to bring a new level of technology, precision and performance to oral care, helping people achieve better oral health outcomes through a more effective daily routine," she continued.

"As with many Dyson innovations, our goal is not simply to improve an existing product, but to rethink the category and challenge conventional approaches."

According to Turney, electric toothbrushes were seen as an area with potential for improvement, since the majority of people do not clean their teeth as effectively as dentists suggest.

"Oral care stood out because, despite decades of innovation elsewhere, people continue to struggle with effective routines," said Turney.

Read:

Dyson's first toothbrush "uses a camera to floss while you brush"

"Flossing compliance remains low, many people miss the areas where plaque first forms, and oral health issues affect billions of people globally," she continued.

"We saw an opportunity to rethink the category from first principles and develop a technology-led solution to help improve everyday oral care habits."

The brand, which has been developing the toothbrush for six years, aimed to shift the process of teeth cleaning by combining brushing and flossing into one action.

To do this, a jet was included in the head of the toothbrush, which sprays mouthwash into gaps between teeth directed by a camera.

"Most electric toothbrushes focus solely on brushing and leave interdental cleaning, the gaps between teeth where plaque often accumulates, to a separate flossing step," said Turney.

"The Dyson CameraJet is designed to do both simultaneously," she continued.

"Rather than asking users to add another step to their routine, it combines brushing and interdental cleaning in one device. Our goal is to make effective oral care easier and more consistent by helping users clean the areas most commonly missed during brushing."

According to Dyson, the camera system was trained on 470,000 dental images to recognise gaps between teeth. Using an artificial intelligence-powered algorithm, it takes 28 images per second to track the teeth and predict gaps.

Dyson said that 661 engineers worked on the project over its development, with the toothbrush tested using a proxy plaque that was developed in collaboration with the National University of Singapore's dentistry faculty.

Along with headphones, Dyson recently created the "world's slimmest vacuum cleaner".

item.content:encoded:
Luffu Link is a sleek, wireless wristband designed to track multiple users at once, conceived by wearable technology company Fitbit to "bring your family's health and safety together".

Available in onyx black, halo gold and sterling blue, the wristband features a metallic double-barrelled body connected to a minimalist strap and has a battery life of up to five days.

The lightweight wearable is the first physical component of the AI-powered Luffu app, which James Park and Eric Friedman of Google-owned Fitbit designed to gather the separate movements of a family and subsequently combine their health data.

Designed to be worn individually by a group of family members, each user's data is communicated via the app.

The screenless wristband features a singular voice-controlled button, fitted to record "everyday health details" ranging from information on symptoms and medications to mood changes and meal plans.

Luffu Link also continuously captures its user's background activity, including sleep patterns and calories burned each day, as well as their resting heart and breathing rates.

The wristband's built-in GPS facilitates location sharing between families, alerting users when individuals enter or leave designated areas.

Double-pressing the wearable's button can also send a "simple check-in" to selected family members, saving the need to contact them by phone.

Park and Friedman were motivated to create the Luffu products after learning that almost one in four adults in the USA are family caregivers, according to a recent report that claimed this figure has risen by almost 50 per cent in the last decade.

Read:

Google combines "smarts and helpfulness" with first smartwatch

Their hope is that by wearing wristbands, families can sync their health and safety data to streamline their communication and close "a major gap" in consumer health tools.

"Families are still piecing together information across wearables, patient portals, medication lists, calendars, notes, text threads, location apps and other disconnected tools," said the duo.

The pair explained that they wanted to avoid designing wristbands that look like "bulky personal safety devices", noting that while the Luffu app is compatible with existing individual wearables, Luffu Link was created to enhance the experience.

Park and Friedman also considered the Luffu products' use of AI to collect data.

"Advances in AI have made it possible to capture information far more simply and naturally, using voice, text, photos and connected data, while also understanding how those signals relate to one another over time," said the duo.

"It's proactive intelligence designed to help families understand what matters and what to do next, not AI added for AI's sake," they claimed.

The world of wearable technology is ever-evolving. In June, tech giant Meta released its first in-house-designed AI smart glasses, with one of the three styles created in collaboration influencer Kylie Jenner – a much-debated launch that we discussed on our Dezeen Weekly podcast.

The images are courtesy of Luffu.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: construction systems manufacturer Ryno's TerraSmart Lattice Rail System was chosen to connect the planting, balustrading, seating and entertainment spaces for interior studio Thirdway Group's rooftop terrace without penetrating the waterproofing.

Ryno's system is a single integrated support structure, created to allow for multiple design elements to be seamlessly coordinated without structural constraints.

The system incorporates Ryno's BaseLink – a freestanding connection component that allows a terrace's balustrades to be secured directly to the supporting structure without penetrating the roof waterproofing.

It also allows for multiple surface finishes to be added, including the brand's Vitrified Composite decking system.

As part of Thirdway's rooftop development, ledge and contour planters were added to accommodate integrated seating and provide access to rainwater outlets.

According to Ryno, this ensured maintenance requirements were added to the design without affecting the terrace's visual appearance.

LED downlighting was also integrated into the planter system to "enhance the atmosphere" for evening use, extending the space's usability beyond working hours.

A late addition to the design process was the addition of a bar area, which was originally omitted due to additional structural supports.

Ryno explained that as an extension to the completed terrace, the planter design was altered to accommodate the feature with minimal disruption.

According to Thirdway, utilising Ryno's freestanding balustrade connection component allowed for Ryno's Linear Track system to be integrated directly into the decking and paving, eliminating the need for additional steelwork or disturbing the waterproofing system.

According to the project team, the flexibility of Ryno's integrated terrace system allowed design decisions to remain open for longer than would typically be possible on a rooftop project.

An access gate was similarly connected directly to the terrace structure using the brand's integrated fixing baseplate, avoiding the need for separate structural steelwork.

The completed terrace now functions as an outdoor extension of Thirdway's headquarters, providing a space for informal meetings, events and day-to-day employee use.

Together with the new headquarters, it reflects Thirdway's commitment to investing in both its people and its clients, with the terrace providing the perfect setting to bring that vision to life.

"It demonstrates how integrated rooftop systems can give designers greater freedom to realise ambitious rooftop environments while reducing coordination challenges between trades, suppliers and specialist contractors," said Ryno.

item.content:encoded:
New York artist Justin Blinder has created a device that slows the city's paid-share bikes as they pass through parts of the city that are under "greater housing pressure".

For the Ground Truth project, Blinder combined his backgrounds in data and design as well as his experience as a bike messenger to create a 3D-printed device that manipulates the brakes of a Citi Bike.

The device slows it down in areas where rent burden, the percentage of a household's income spent on rent and utilities, is high.

"The city stopped feeling like a map and started to feel like the sequence of really radically different conditions that I was encountering," Blinder told Dezeen.

This led the artist to ask, "what if affordability wasn't something you mapped onto the city, but became part of the terrain you actually had to move through?"

The project seeks to physicalize housing data.

"It's very hard to understand visually what affordability looks like with all of the complex policies embedded in the built environment," Blinder said.

"That idea was very much present in these preconceptions I had while I was biking throughout the city delivering food, especially with what affordable housing often ends up looking like, how people who are rent burdened are depicted, or people who live in NYCHA housing are represented in rent burden datasets."

Blinder primarily used data from the American Community Survey for the project, combining the median share of income spent on rent and the percentage of renter households spending at least half of their income on housing, according to his website dedicated to the project.

His research and data models are stored in the device, which in turn "applies tension" to the front brakes as a biker passes through the city.

"In areas with greater housing pressure, it applies more resistance; in more affordable areas, it releases that tension," reads a project description.

The small, grey machine clamps onto the front fork of a CitiBike. Blinder said he worked with an industrial designer on its creation and designed it to be installed with minimal effort.

A tiny screen displays the local rent burden percentile as riders pass through the area, and a QR code that leads to the project website.

Read:

Riksbyggen creates Sweden's smallest apartments to "make the housing crisis tangible"

Building it was "maybe the easiest part of the project", according to Blinder. The artist says it consists of four main parts – a tiny computer called an ESP32S3, an SD card with Blinder's dataset, a GPS system and a servo motor with a tiny arm attached to it that reaches out to control the brakes.

According to the artist, the data is highly localised and can change even between blocks. Blinder also noted that Citi Bike docks themselves can illustrate differences in the city based on where they are available.

"Urban infrastructure isn't just experienced functionally – it's also experienced symbolically as a set of different social signals about who places are for, who it's being redesigned for, and what kind of changes are coming in the future, and so the same bike lane or city bike dock can signify access or safety to one person, but also displacement to someone else."

Blinder said that, for safety reasons, the device is not fixed to any public bikes. Instead, he's organised group tours where volunteers can experience the project with the help of sponsor Idle Hands, a Brooklyn-based incubator.

He said he hopes to eventually transform the project into an open-source resource, where others can create their own Ground Truth device.

"A lot of my projects try to take traditional representations and problematize them, make them a bit less stable, and to take the data off the screen and really put it back in contact with the streets, our bodies, and a lot of the assumptions we have about places and the built environment," said Blinder.

Conceptual tools for bringing awareness to affordability were also recently used in Sweden with tiny housing units by Developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO.

Earlier this year, an ADU initiative was rolled out by New York mayor Zohran Mamdani in light of ongoing affordability issues in the city,

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studios MAD and Stantec have placed more than 1,200 curved panels on the "dream-like" Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, which is set to open later this month.

Set in a 13-acre site near Los Angeles' Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is a five-storey structure dedicated to storytelling and founded by Star Wars creator George Lucas and businesswoman Mellody Hobson.

The museum has an elongated form that narrows in the middle with 1,271 white, fibre-glass-reinforced polymer panels covering its facade to give it a smooth, almost spaceship-like appearance. The panels measure 8 by 32 feet (2.4 by 9.7 metres) on average.

According to MAD founder Ma Yansong, the structure was "designed with emotional architecture space, so that it is fluid in every part".

The edges of the structure cantilever beyond its supports, furthering the space ship analogy.

Arches, formed at select places along the facade where the panelling tapers, are filled with glass.

MAD said that the form and cantilevers work together to make the structure appear to be floating.

"The biomorphic form of the building is designed to cantilever far beyond the support of where the building touches the ground to give he impression that the building is floating over the park," said the studio.

Yet, Yansong said that the studio was also meant to merge "like a natural feature of the landscape" and be inviting for guests.

Though the structure does feel extraterrestrial and gigantic compared to the surroundings, the landscaping, carried out by California practice Studio-MLA, does help weave it into the adjacent park. This is further aided by greenery on the sections of the roof not covered by photovoltaic panels.

"The museum's reflective approach encourages a fluid transition between indoor and outdoor realms, reflecting humans' innate tendency to seek connections with nature," said MAD.

"The museum's biomorphic, dream-like form features fluid and soft shapes creating a distinctive and recognizable landmark and offering an immersive experience that explores the relationship between nature, society, and the urban environment."

In the centre of the structure is the semi-enclosed plaza. The space is covered by a structure, which was made from 185-foot-long steel beams, that supports a massive oculus.

From the plaza, visitors enter the vast lobbies on either side. One features wooden cladding, while the other is clad in more curving white panels. The latter has three cylindrical glass elevators to bring visitors up into the body of the structure, which sit in front of a pair of 299-seat theatres.

The lower two floors contain a horseshoe-shaped library that looks out into the landscape as well as classrooms, a shop and cafe.

On the fourth floor are the bulk of the gallery spaces. These extend through the middle of the structure, where visitors can look down through the oculus.

On the fifth floor, there are more gallery spaces as well as a Rockwell Group-designed restaurant, called Skywalker Grill, with fluted wood detailing mixing with the white panelling.

Compared with the white expanses of the exterior and lobbies, some of the galleries themselves, designed by WHY Architecture, are quite traditional. Though at some points, the curved panelling system is brought in again, especially in the Stars Wars sections.

A mix of art from recreations of ancient cave paintings to Renaissance works and Star Wars props are arranged in white-walled spaces with wooden mosaic parquet floors.

"The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art was created to honor humanity's stories and the artists who illustrate them," said Lucas.

"The artists in this collection didn't just create images, they connected our modern imaginations with our ancient emotions—with common beliefs creating community," he continued.

"Their work spans genres, media, and time."

At some places in the gallery, the raw concrete is exposed on the ceiling, gridded by white-metal beams for track lighting and overhead modular wall support.

On a more practical note, the architecture studio emphasised the seismic durability of the structure. It has 281 seismic base isolators as well as a "moat" that surrounds the ground floor and allows the ground around the building to move with the motion of an earthquake.

Read:

MAD scatters boulder-like galleries across green-roofed museum in Shenzhen

The grounds themselves are heavily designed and also feature artworks.

Studio-MLA said it also wanted the grounds to play into the storytelling theme that carries through the whole of the museum.

"We thought of the visitor as a traveler, drawing on California's dramatic terrain – foothills, valleys, mesas, canyons, meadows—to create a journey in which topography, planting, and light shift the way setting shifts a story," said the studio.

"Sculpted over the underground parking structure, the topography negotiates changes in elevation while creating varied microhabitats; paths climb, descend, and cross bridges, with no single route through the gardens."

The structure broke ground in 2018 and will open to the public on 22 September.

MAD is known for its monumental structures and was named one of Dezeen's 2025 Designers of the Year. Also in California, the studio completed a condo building in Beverly Hills with what was America's "largest living wall" at the time.

item.content:encoded:
A takeover of Richmond's Ham House and Garden, a sound installation at Wapping Hydraulic Power Station and a group show of 102 emerging designers are among the highlights at this year's London Design Festival.

The programme for this year's festival, running from 12 to 20 September, is one of the strongest we've seen since the pandemic, bringing together stalwarts like SCP and Gallery Fumi with a slew of self-organised shows from young and up-and-coming talent.

Read on for Dezeen's pick of the 14 events not to miss.

Awakenings at the Victoria & Albert Museum

Artificial intelligence takes centre stage at the V&A. As part of this year's Emerging Design Commission, Playfool presents a game reflecting on human labour in the age of AI, while an installation from Nina Davies examines how human bodies are starting to mimic AI-generated movement.

Taking a more positive view is Aziza Kaydri's Sender Unknown, which combines Uzbek embroidery techniques with a bespoke Al model.

Similar themes are explored at Craft x Tech, which pairs Japanese craftspeople with international designers to reinterpret traditional techniques through contemporary design, with this year's cohort including Philippe Malouin and Bethan Laura Wood (above).

12 September to 18 October. Cromwell Road, SW7 2RL.

Design Everything at Aram

Non-profit collective Design Everything hopes to visualise the many barriers faced by independent creatives in London with its show at Aram. The shop's downstairs gallery has been transformed into the typical flat of a young designer, populated exclusively with objects made by 102 emerging practitioners.

Selected via an open call that received more than 500 responses, each piece was created in response to a limitation – space, time, budget, access. Design Everything hopes that the free-to-exhibit show will serve as an "important point of reflection on the current state of the industry" while also celebrating designers' indelible ability to turn restrictions into a source of inspiration.

Upstairs, Aram is also hosting a free-to-use coworking space, offering a place to work, meet and recharge during the week, as well as a pop-up from historic Italian design brand Arflex, bringing together seminal products and new releases making their UK debut.

11 September to 10 October. 110 DruryLane, WC2B 5SG.

SCP showroom opening

Furniture brand SCP celebrates its move from Shoreditch to Clerkenwell with a programme of launches and events across its new five-storey townhouse, with interiors by Nice Projects.

On show is a collection of ceramic vases by Martino Gamper and Italian manufacturer Bitossi Ceramiche, a new lighting collection by Manhattan studio Blue Green Works and the UK launch of Italian brand Very Simple: Kitchen (above).

12 to 19 September. SCP, 16 Clerkenwell Green, ECIR OQT.

The Lavery at Cromwell Place

The Lavery is once again hosting a packed programme, in which Brompton Design District curator Alex Tieghi-Walker introduces Londoners to international names to know alongside homegrown talent.

Fresh from its debut exhibition at Saatchi Yates, makeup artist and creative director Isamaya Ffrench's design gallery Studio Iron (above) presents a new group exhibition from a melting pot of independent makers, including Dutch designer Paul Coenen, Iranian-American furnituremaker Kouros Maghsoud and interior designer Kelly Wearstler.

Elsewhere at The Lavery, creative director Beverly Nguyen shares an exhibition of Vietnamese domestic objects, while Nigerian-American designer Zoë Ene has reimagined one of the rooms as a parlour for playing the strategy game Nchọ. Mexican designer Rafael Prieto takes over the dining room with a series of sculptural chairs inspired by positions of the sun.

And in nearby Cromwell Mews, furnituremaker Byron Pritchard showcases furniture informed by research into medieval woodworking at the V&A.

12 to 20 September. The Lavery, 4 Cromwell Place, SW7 2JE.

The Art of Sound at Wapping Hydraulic Power Station

The historic Wapping Hydraulic Power Station is opening its doors to the public for the first time in 13 years to host an immersive sound experience.

French manufacturer L-Acoustics has created a system of 12 speakers especially for the venue, filling the halls of the 1890 industrial icon with a sound installation from computational biologist Max Cooper, as well as an auditory journey down the Humber estuary courtesy of award-winning sound recordist Chris Watson.

11 to 15 September. 25 Wapping Wall, EIW 3SF.

Past Made Present exhibition at Ham House

Richmond's 17th-century Ham House provides a dramatic backdrop for this exhibition from graduates of Kingston University's MA Product and Furniture Design programme. The show offers visitors new ways of engaging with the history, interiors and gardens of the property.

Highlights include a contemporary throne exploring colonial histories through reinterpreted Dutch marquetry (top image by Luke Alexander), Coade stone objects that act as viewfinders for forgotten architectural details and a speaker cabinet inspired by the house's Japanese lacquer cabinets and modern listening bar culture.

12 to 20 September. Ham House and Garden, Ham Street, TW1O 7RS.

Material Matters fair

London's materials fair has found a new home in Shoreditch for its fifth edition, bringing together more than 50 exhibitors showcasing natural, reclaimed and newly developed materials.

Among the highlights: furniture crafted using salvaged oak from a brutalist building in Holborn courtesy of design studio Prima Materia (above), bacteria-grown tiles inspired by coral from biotech company Biomason and a 3D-printed ceramic facade system designed to integrate wildlife habitats into buildings by design studio Phyta Biodesign.

15 to 17 September. Unlocked Shoreditch, 118 Curtain Road, EC2A 3PJ.

Max Radford Gallery at Christopher Farr

London's buzziest collectible design gallery is taking over Christopher Farr's Shoreditch showroom, with an exhibition pairing contemporary furniture and archival rugs.

It features works by London designers LS Goma (above) and Tessa Silva that have never actually been shown in their home town before, alongside pieces from rising German star Carsten in der Elst.

15 to 20 September. Christopher Farr Shoreditch, 18 Calvin Street, E1 6HF.

Made x Barbican launch

One of London's most recognisable architectural icons has received its own furniture collection courtesy of furniture brand Made. Drawing on the Barbican's original interiors and architectural details, the 23-piece collection also includes lighting, textiles and accessories.

On the ground floor of the Barbican Centre, an installation delves into the design process, exploring how the estate's original layouts and show home interiors by architect Miriam Howitt informed the collection.

12 to 20 September. Barbican Centre, Silk Street, EC2Y 8DS.

Village Meeting group show by All Ears

A number of practices are opening up their workshops in Hackney Downs Studios as part of LDF. Rather than just spotlighting its own work, East London duo All Ears is hosting Village Meeting – a group show of more than 30 makers from London's emerging collectible design scene.

Look out for works from Milan design week standouts Jane Wright and Jesse Butterfield, ashtray connoisseur Amelia Stevens and Andu Masebo (fresh off the heels of his IKEA collaboration), as well as the show's curator Demi Oyeyinka.

16 to 20 September. All Ears, Hackney Downs Studios, 17 Amhurst Terrace, E8 2BT.

The Pangolin Shield installation by Studio Saar and Atelier One

Architecture practice Studio Saar and engineering firm Atelier One have collaborated on this year's Landmark Project – a bamboo pavilion inspired by the world's most trafficked mammal, the pangolin.

Clad in traditional Indian bamboo police shields and palm-leaf rain covers known as knups (above), the installation transforms symbols of authority into a communal space for reflection while examining colonial legacies and ecological exploitation.

12 to 20 September. Strand Aldwych, WC2R 1ES.

After School show by Gallery Fumi X RCA

Gallery Fumi partners with the Royal College of Art to present After School, a selection of outstanding work by recent alumni, spanning textiles, ceramics and design.

Outside of the Mayfair gallery, graduates of the MA Design Products degree are presenting their final year projects at RCA's Kensington campus, while just down the road at Thurloe Place, the One Tool, One Stool exhibition shares outcomes from the first exercise they undertook as fledgling design students: creating a stool using only a single tool.

12 to 26 September. Gallery Fumi, 2-3 Hay Hill, WIJ 6AS.

Hanging Baskets and Travel Light shows by Slancha

The humble hanging basket has been reimagined by 10 designers as part of an exhibition at Awaykin from emerging design gallery Slancha. The show's UK-heavy roster includes metalwork studio Six Dots Design, Scottish designer Marc Sweeney and This IsByron (above).

Slancha is also taking over the gift shop at The Hoxton with pieces submitted by newer talents from more than 20 countries. Drawing on references from Welsh love spoons to Ugandan barkcloth, all the pieces are available to buy at accessible price points.

14 to 20 September at Awaykin, Unit 5, 39 Gransden Avenue, E8 3QA.
12 to 20 September at The Hoxton, 81 Great Eastern St, EC2A 3HU.

You Can Sit With Us exhibition by 2LG Studio

Interiors firm 2LG Studio's always excellent showcase of emerging design talent has returned to Shoreditch Town Hall for its fourth edition.

This year's lineup includes one of Milan design week's breakout stars, reformed production designer Jabez Bartlett, alongside Hanna Fastrich, Mara Bragagnolo (above), JoshJen and more, while 2LG Studio will also debut a new lighting collection with Indian studio North South AD.

While you're at Shoreditch Town Hall, check out the wider House of Icon exhibition, which also includes a show from Italian design platform Isola.

15 to 17 September. Shoreditch Town Hall, 380 Old Street, ECIV 9LT.

item.content:encoded:
Preservation body Historic England and the City of London are in dispute over the impact future skyscraper development will have on the Tower of London.

In the latest hearing to determine the City Plan 2040, Historic England explained that it believes clear sky is needed between the Tower of London and the City of London in order to protect the historic landmark.

"Reducing the potential for harm is of vital importance"

Historic England, the government's statutory adviser on the historic environment, claims that plans to build offices at the eastern edge of the City of London would be a threat to the Tower of London's UNESCO heritage status.

"We are keen to work together to identify solutions to reduce the potential for further harm to the Tower of London World Heritage Site whilst still achieving major economic growth," said a Historic England spokesperson.

"Reducing the potential for harm is of vital importance to the conservation of the World Heritage Site, and we believe critical to minimising the potential for the Tower of London to be included on the List of World Heritage in Danger."

Built on the River Thames by king William I in the 11th century, the Tower of London is recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Read:

Llowarch Llowarch Architects completes raven enclosure for the Tower of London

Hearings on the City Plan 2040, which will determine the growth of London's financial district, resumed following UK minister for housing and planning Matthew Pennycook's request for further consideration of the plan's impact on the Tower of London.

In June, Pennycook sought reassurances that the plan "does everything it can to protect the tower adequately against the risk of unsuitable or harmful development whilst not unduly restricting economic growth".

This caused delays to the City of London Corporation publishing the plan, which aims include a target for a minimum of 1.2 million square metres of additional office space to be built in the area.

Restriction would "harm growth without good reason"

The City of London claims that Historic England's request to create space between the castle and the district would result in a loss of crucial office development space.

"The Government has said it wants good growth in every postcode – the City's postcodes are the most economically productive in the country," said chair of the City of London planning and transportation committee Tom Sleigh.

"To harm their growth without good reason at a time of national economic urgency would be like entering a race with your shoelaces tied together. The City has grown alongside the Tower of London for nine centuries; the two have never been a choice," he continued.

"This plan makes room for the offices London needs and respects the Tower's setting – that is the balance the minister has asked the inspectors to test, and we are confident it holds. After that, business needs a decision, and soon."

item.content:encoded:
US furniture brand Emeco has begun legal action against Zara Home for allegedly copying a chair and a stool designed for the brand by architect Norman Foster.

Emeco filed the lawsuit in the Hamburg District Court, Germany, earlier this year, alleging that Spanish brand Zara Home had "unlawfully copied the appearance and protected design language" of pieces in its 20-06 collection.

The furniture brand alleges that Zara Home's Stainless Steel Structure Chair and Stainless Steel Bar Stool infringe on the design of its 20-06 Chair and 20-06 Stool.

"We are committed to protecting original design and the integrity of the creative and manufacturing process," said Emeco chairman Gregg Buchbinder.

Dezeen has contacted Zara Home regarding the accusation, but the brand declined to comment.

Lawsuit seeks production halt and damages

Released in 2006, the Emeco pieces were designed by Foster + Partners founder Foster as a modern version of the brand's 1006 Navy Chair, which was developed in 1944 for the United States Navy.

Both the Emeco and Zara Home pieces include a chair and a stool in a metal finish with a seat that curves over the legs at the front.

The legs and frame of Emeco's 20-06 collection pieces are constructed from square tubes made from 80-per-cent-recycled aluminium, while the Zara Home pieces are made from round stainless-steel tubes.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Milenyum Metal (@milenyummetal_)

Zara Home Stainless Steel Structure Chair was made from stainless steel

According to Emeco, it issued cease-and-desist and damages claims to Zara Home before filing the lawsuit. However, the brand said that Zara Home declined its request to cease manufacture of its pieces.

The lawsuit seeks damages and to stop Zara Home from selling the Stainless Steel Structure Chair and Stainless Steel Bar Stool.

"Companies like Emeco become unpaid research and development laboratories"

Emeco said that the practice of large companies producing versions of well-selling design pieces exploits smaller brands.

"Massive international chains often appropriate the intellectual property of smaller companies to reduce risk, accelerate speed to market, and avoid the enormous investment required for innovation," said Buchbinder.

"Large retailers often wait until a design has already proven itself in the marketplace before copying it," he continued.

"By doing so, they avoid the uncertainty, development costs, and years of market education required to establish an original product. In effect, companies like Emeco become unpaid research and development laboratories for global chains."

The photography is courtesy of Emeco.

Dezeen Showroom: Istanbul and London-based Yet Design Studio has launched a matching pouf and table made from aluminium angle profiles commonly used in construction.

The Strut table and pouf join Yet Design Studio's Strut chair, which launched during the 2025 edition of Milan Design Week, to form the three-piece collection.

Yet describes the pouf as having a "compact yet confident form", comprising a circular leather-upholstered seat – available in black or white – as well as a drum-like cylindrical body and a base tucked beneath fashioned from faceted aluminium profiles.

"Though intimate in scale, the Strut Pouf expresses a strong sense of clarity and character, demonstrating how simple geometric forms can convey both strength and beauty," said Yet.

The table, through its sharp-cornered square top and rigid legs at each corner, "extends the collection's structural idea into a shared horizontal plane".

"The supporting elements are not treated as secondary details; they define the visual identity of the object itself," said Yet.

"Strut began with a question: can the element that carries an object also become the source of its character? The collection grew from that question, allowing one structural idea to take on different scales, functions and expressions," said designer Yağmur Köylü.

Created in collaboration with local manufacturer Floor

item.content:encoded:
Design practice POOR Collective has unveiled Power, two flatwoven rugs informed by the brutalist Trellick Tower housing block, which will be on display at London Design Festival.

Power is the first mass-produced design product from London-based POOR Collective, a socially minded creative practice with a community development focus.

Created in collaboration with local manufacturer Floor Story, the collection features a duo of rugs in two colourways – evergreen and tangerine.

Each piece was flat-woven with warp and weft yarns of New Zealand wool, patterned with intersecting geometric shapes that nod to the angular architecture of Ernö Goldfinger's iconic Trellick Tower.

Completed in 1972 and located on west London's Golborne Road, the housing estate's varied legacy was POOR Collective's starting point for the collection.

"Trellick Tower felt like a natural choice for us to draw on because it has such a strong visual identity," collective co-founder and designer Ben Spry told Dezeen.

"But also, because of the social history and cultural significance attached to it. It's a building that has been through a lot of different perceptions over its lifetime," he continued.

"That felt relevant to POOR because so much of our work is about challenging assumptions about places and communities, and thinking about how design can contribute to a different narrative."

Handwoven in India, the rectangular rugs will be on display during this month's upcoming London Design Festival (LDF) as part of an exhibition at Floor Story's London showroom.

Power was a full collaboration between Spry, fellow collective members Akmaral Khassen, Shawn Adams, Larry Botchway and Matt Harvey-Agyemang, as well as Floor Story designer Gill Thorpe.

Read:

Eight projects by POOR Collective that reimagine co-design as "a two-way street"

Previously, the collective has focussed on more site-specific projects including the colourful renovation of a south London games court and a covered pavilion designed to draw attention to the realities faced by urban night-shift workers.

But Power marks the group's debut mass-produced product conceived for a brand.

Spry explained why this new direction is meaningful for the collective.

"POOR has always been interested in making design accessible and putting it into people's everyday lives, so the opportunity to take something that has come out of our design practice and make it available to a much wider audience felt like a really exciting progression," said the designer.

"A lot of our work is commissioned and site-specific, often involving a particular community or place," he added.

"We love that, but it can also mean that the work exists in one location and is experienced by a relatively small number of people. A product has a different kind of reach. It can enter people's homes and become part of their everyday environment."

The photography is by Mark Cocksedge.

item.content:encoded:
Chinese interior designer Bin Wu's book Timeless East explores the idea of a design language rooted in the philosophical context of the East. For this roundup, he picks six of his own favourite projects in China and abroad.

The Design Language of Timeless East features 17 projects completed by Wu and his studio W Design, spanning interior design, art installations and design research.

Wu's aim was to challenge the absence of Eastern voices from modern design narratives. Instead, he hoped to show Eastern design through a different lens that would be more true to its original roots and promote a spiritual connection.

"Whether it was the Japonisme of the nineteenth century or the Chinoiserie of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, these were projections of the Eastern imagination filtered through a Western lens – not distillations of Eastern culture and art articulated by the East itself," Wu told Dezeen.

"Even in the wake of China's rapid economic ascent over the past two decades, this predicament remains unresolved," he continued. "The Design Language of Timeless East is a response issued from the Eastern subject itself."

Here, Dezeen selects six projects from the book that explore the Timeless East design language:

Hai Shang restaurant, Shanghai, 2023

At this fusion restaurant in Shanghai, Wu combined raw materials with a dark colour palette to create a subtle atmosphere with a mysterious feel.

Sea reeds are stacked into a circular enclosure at the entrance, which leads to a narrow corridor paved with rustic stone. This was designed to be reminiscent of old Chinese water towns – historic towns known for their bridges and rivers – and opens up to an open kitchen.

The studio kept the exposed beams to reveal the history of the building, while adding a countertop crafted from a massive ink stone.

The Fame, Chengdu, 2024

Wu designed this visitor centre for a residential complex in Chengdu, using locally sourced materials to evoke the experience of wandering in a garden.

The entrance hall was clad with bamboo strips that allow light to filter through the gaps, creating a constantly shifting interplay of light and shadow.

Connecting corridors weave together various open spaces, creating a fluid and ever-changing atmosphere that aligns with the Chinese garden principle of "not revealing everything at once".

The main social space features dark terracotta panels on the wall that were designed to resemble local roof tiles in a nod to the rustic mountain dwellings nearby.

Deqin Meri Poodom Hotel, Deqin, 2024

Located at the foot of Meri Snow Mountain, a sacred place for the local Tibetan community, this hotel design aims to balance spirituality and everyday living.

Wu designed its central staircase to evoke a white pagoda – a historic building of religious significance. He created its encased and overlapping stairs, each turning at a forty-five-degree angle, for visitors to feel like they are climbing towards the sky.

Locally relevant objects were incorporated into the interiors, including yak bells and black pottery. All guest rooms frame part of the Meri Mountain, which has 13 sacred peaks in total, to make visitors feel closer to the heart of Tibetan faith.

Collector's Mansion, Shanghai, 2024

W Design completed the facade renovation, as well as a display apartment, for this luxury residential complex in Shanghai's former French Concession.

Orderly arranged balconies add a sense of rhythm to the otherwise clean, minimalist facade. Inside the apartment, the living room opens up after a narrow foyer.

The interiors have a restrained colour and material palette to create a tranquil atmosphere and include tactile furniture with rough surfaces designed to resemble old objects.

Pan Yuan: Momentality Unfold, Milan, 2024

Wu revealed this paper installation during Milan Design Week 2024.

Located in the central courtyard of the Cortile d'Onore at the University of Milan, the installation reflected the Eastern architectural emphasis on change, seeking eternity within impermanence.

Based on the theme "momentality", it used large-scale paper scrolls, a material commonly found in Eastern architecture and painting, to form an Eastern garden experience that contrasted the surrounding historical architecture.

The installation was made from lightweight and durable DuPont Tyvek paper, which has a texture that strongly resembles traditional Eastern Xuan paper.

Arbour, Shanghai, 2025

W Design created a quietly elegant "indoor theatre" for this residence in Shanghai, where soft lighting, a spiral staircase, and refined vintage furnishings evoke a sense of nostalgia.

Drapes were used across dining rooms and bedrooms to soften the spatial boundaries, while wood furniture and timber flooring add warmth to the space.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: global commercial design studios, including JLL Design, are using AI floor plan generator laiout to "evaluate more layout options earlier".

laiout launched in 2021 to change how commercial space is planned by improving the early stages of the design process. The generator is described as a "complete, end-to-end office space planning platform", differentiating it from a rendering tool, BIM integration or single-purpose test-fit generator.

According to the company, by switching to laiout, work that once took days across multiple disconnected tools can now be completed in a single automated workflow.

The AI software is now used to generate more than five million square metres of commercial space each month, including in JLL Design's 65 global studios, where laiout was recently adopted.

"As a designer myself, I know how much creativity gets lost to mundane, repetitive processes," said Cristiano Coretti, chief product officer at laiout. "Automating that work doesn't reduce design – it gives designers more room to do what only they can do."

The company explained that laiout generates the first draft, with designers shaping the final space in minutes afterwards.

Here, division of labour "is not a compromise – it's where design quality and commercial performance meet".

"Our starting point with any new platform is a straightforward question: does this solve a real problem in our design process at the scale we operate?" said JLL Design global design operations lead Romeu Carpinteiro.

laiout quickly generates usable office layouts based on real-world, site-specific constraints.

"Early-stage space planning involves significant constraint-solving work, building codes, capacity calculations, and compliance checks that consume time before creative design decisions can begin," explained Carpinteiro.

"When we evaluated laiout, we were looking for a platform that could handle that systematic work reliably across different markets, freeing our designers to focus on decisions that require human judgment and spatial expertise," he added.

According to laiout, dramatically reducing the time it takes to create an initial office layout means design teams have more time to amend and iterate the designs to better suit the client's needs.

At JLL Design, the studio explained they have experienced a marked shift in how design teams spend their time.

"The measurable change with laiout is in how our teams allocate their time," explained Carpinteiro. "We can now evaluate more layout options earlier in the design process, respond to competitive briefs faster, and redirect designer hours toward refinement and client engagement rather than production of initial options."

JLL Design's studio survey recorded a 50 per cent reduction in test-fit time following adoption of laiout. Following successful pilots that demonstrated consistent performance across multiple markets and building types, JLL Design rolled out laiout across every design studio globally last month.

According to the studio, laiout has also been adopted across multiple departments, including Occupancy Planning.

In practice, that means test fits that once took days can now take as little as a few minutes, up to 40 minutes on average. JLL Design explained that as a result, teams can pursue more opportunities, respond to competitive briefs faster, and are quicker to win deals.

"We've spent years building our own algorithms to create a platform that has been independently measured to cut production time by up to 93 per cent, depending on project complexity and how far a team is into adoption, " said laiout CEO Wouter Merkestein.

"Designers tell us the quick iteration sparks their creativity, while freeing up time for details they previously couldn't get to. Quality goes up as time spent goes down."

laiout is used in over 46 countries and across every JLL Design studio globally.

According to the company, it has grown organically, market by market, rather than through a single top-down decision.

To learn more about laiout, visit its website.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: Villeroy & Boch has published several of its new bathroom products on Dezeen Showroom, highlighting creative and sophisticated tapware, basins and vanity units.

Among the products is the Vea tapware, a lever-less design by German industrial designer Christian Haas based on his search for what he describes as "sensual reduction".

Haas looked to the design language of classic perfume bottles for the faceted design, which is available in black or white ceramic.

The form is intended to be sculptural yet calm and capable of blending into different bathroom settings, with one central button in place of a lever reducing visual noise.

A bold basin design comes from Roberto Palomba for Villeroy & Boch subsidiary Ideal Standard, who together have created Tipo-Z, a statuesque pedestal basin with a tapered, aerodynamic-looking silhouette.

Available in black or white, the basin is made of Ideal Standard's durable fireclay material, which allows for the realisation of its precisely defined edges.

Other new products from Villeroy & Boch use a new material developed with German design studio KaschKasch using 100 per cent recycled ceramic that is 3D printed.

Titled Antao 3D, the material is made entirely from the company's own production waste and carries subtle variations created in the process of layered printing.

The material builds on KaschKasch and Villeroy & Boch's Antao collection, which is focused on bringing elements from nature into the bathroom and also celebrates the beauty of imperfection.

Their recent Antao Earth washbasins showcase this approach. They have a dewdrop-shaped form and hand-glazed finish, with resulting variations in colour and texture giving a tactile appeal.

A further contribution from Haas comes in the form of two new product additions to Villeroy & Boch's colour-focused Artis collection: Artis Sense and Artis Frame.

Artis Sense is a surface-mounted washbasin with a delicate expression inspired by textiles, while Artis Frame is a complementary bathroom furniture design bringing the lightweight, modern look of open metal shelving.

Villeroy & Boch is one of Europe's oldest and most respected names in ceramics, with a history stretching back 278 years and involving the merger of two great German ceramics families.

Today, the company focuses on two divergent ceramics categories – bathroom products and tableware – but always with a focus on innovative design and manufacturing.

Take a short tour of the recently opened Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, USA, is this video filmed by Dezeen.

Designed by US studio Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects to honour US president Barack Obama, the complex in the South Side of Chicago opened to the public in June.

This short video shows a visit to the presidential centre, which includes a 69-metre-tall (226-feet-tall), granite-clad tower, plaza and public library.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dezeen (@dezeen)

This video shows inside the Obama Presidential Center

The monumental tower contains a multi-floor exhibition, designed by Ralph Appelbaum Associates, dedicated to the former president. It is topped by the Skyroom, which has views across the city.

Alongside the tower are a series of low-lying buildings arranged around a central plaza. These contain a Chicago Public Library branch and a building with an auditorium and large restaurant.

These buildings were topped with landscaping and gardens that connect to the wider Jackson Park, which was designed in the late 19th century by American landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted.

We recently rounded up all of the other presidential libraries across the USA, dedicated to presidents from Herbert Hoover to George W Bush.
